articles.title: MP investiga interferência de facções nas eleições em Forquilha | G1
articles.standfirst: Segundo a Secretaria da Segurança Pública, chega a 13 o total de pessoas detidas desde o início da campanha eleitoral, em 16 de agosto, por tentativa de interferir no pleito no Ceará, sob ordens de facção.
articles.summary: O Ministério Público apura a interferência de facções nas eleições em Forquilha após 13 prisões por ameaças e extorsão contra candidatos no Ceará.
articles.body:
O Ministério Público Eleitoral (MPE) instaurou uma investigação para apurar possível interferência de integrantes de organização criminosa na campanha de candidatos em Forquilha , interior do Ceará. Na cidade, suspeitos foram presos suspeitos de ameaçar e tentar extorquir agentes políticos .

O Procedimento Investigatório Criminal (PIC) foi formalizado após denúncia do prefeito do município. De acordo com o MP, as apurações tiveram início a partir de informações de que integrantes de uma facção criminosa teriam ameaçado candidatos e agentes políticos e buscado influenciar o andamento da campanha no município.

🔎 O PIC é um procedimento instaurado com o objetivo de apurar condutas criminais, servindo como preparação para uma possível ação penal. Pode ser instaurado por iniciativa do próprio MP ou a partir de denúncias, representações ou notícias de fato.

"As condutas podem ter comprometido a liberdade de propaganda eleitoral, a igualdade de condições entre os postulantes e a livre manifestação da vontade dos eleitores. Os elementos coletados até o momento também indicam a possível prática de crimes eleitorais e comuns, como participação dos envolvidos em organização criminosa ultraviolenta", diz o ministério.

Como uma das primeiras medidas da investigação, será colhido depoimento do prefeito no dia 2 de setembro, na sede da Polícia Federal em Sobral. O gestor deverá apresentar documentos, mensagens, áudios, vídeos e outros dados relacionados aos fatos.

"O Ministério Público Eleitoral também requisitou informações a órgãos de segurança pública e autoridades policiais para aprofundar as apurações sobre a atuação da organização criminosa e a possível influência no processo eleitoral do município", informou o órgão.

Membro de facção preso em São Paulo usava perfis nas redes sociais para ameaçar e extorquir de candidatos em Forquilha, no Ceará — Foto: Divulgação

Em Forquilha, no dia 20 de agosto, dois homens foram presos suspeitos de ameaçar e tentar extorquir agentes políticos de Forquilha. Os capturados têm 19 e 28 anos e foram identificados como Gean Barboza Fontenele e Francisco Werlysson Feijão Silva, o “Ratin” . As ameaças foram feitas a pessoas ligadas ao prefeito do município, Edinardo Rodrigues Filho (PSB).

Os homens, apontados como membros do Comando Vermelho, cobraram R$ 200 mil para que candidatos a deputado — aliados ao prefeito — pudessem fazer campanha na cidade. No dia 26, a polícia prendeu, em São Paulo, um homem de 21 anos, membro do Comando Vermelho, suspeito de envolvimento nas práticas de ameaça e extorsão contra candidatos em Forquilha.

No dia 27, a Delegacia de Forquilha deflagrou uma operação para prender envolvidos no esquema no Rio de Janeiro. Um dos presos foi José Álisson Vitorino da Costa, capturado no bairro Leblon. Na sexta-feira (28), uma mulher, de 19 anos, foi presa na cidade de Forquilha. A identidade dela não foi repassada. No entanto, o motivo da prisão dela foi o mesmo dos outros dois suspeitos.

Mais de 10 já foram presos por ameaças contra campanhas eleitorais no Ceará

Segundo a Secretaria de Segurança Pública do Ceará (SSPDS), chega a 13 o total de pessoas detidas desde o início do período eleitoral , em 16 de agosto, por tentativa de interferir no pleito no Ceará, sob ordens de facção.

Nos últimos dias, houve prisões relacionadas a criminosos tentando interferir nas eleições de três municípios: Maranguape , Forquilha e Itapajé.

📌 De modo geral, os membros da facção criminosa usam de artifícios principalmente tecnológicos, como redes sociais e ligações telefônicas, para fazer ameaças, coagir pessoas e cobrar taxas exorbitantes. Em alguns casos, facção impõe taxas de milhares de reais para permitir realização de campanhas. Em outros, os criminosos proíbem a entrada de político em determinadas áreas.

Nos diferentes casos, a Secretaria de Segurança Pública destacou que, graças a dados de inteligência, as forças de segurança do Ceará já realizaram 13 capturas de "suspeitos de integrar organizações criminosas com tentativa de atuação no contexto eleitoral de 2026".

articles.title: Avalanche de lama no Nepal: Moradores buscam cofre e desaparecidos | G1
articles.standfirst: Em cidade devastada pela lama, moradores procuram familiares desaparecidos e tentam recuperar pertences; homem diz acreditar que dinheiro de cofre de banco está intacto.
articles.summary: Após a avalanche de lama no Nepal, moradores de Trichuli enfrentam a destruição para localizar familiares desaparecidos e recuperar pertences em meio aos escombros.
articles.body:
A cidade de Trichuli, no Nepal, foi devastada pela força da água e da lama na última semana. Casas, lojas, uma ponte e parte do centro da cidade foram destruídos. Em meio aos escombros, moradores enfrentam uma corrida contra o tempo para encontrar parentes desaparecidos e recuperar o que ainda pode ser salvo.

No centro da cidade, um morador contou que uma loja estava sendo saqueada, enquanto outro apontou para o local onde estaria o cofre de um banco e disse acreditar que o dinheiro estava intacto . O homem afirmou que tinha a chave e tentava acessar o cofre para retirar o dinheiro.

A cena dá uma dimensão da situação enfrentada pelos moradores: enquanto equipes procuram sobreviventes e famílias buscam notícias de parentes, há também quem tente recuperar bens em uma cidade praticamente destruída.

“Isso aqui era uma cidade inteira que foi pelo rio”, descreve o repórter Felipe Pessanha ao mostrar a área atingida.

Moradores veem a destruição causada por lamaçal no banco da cidade. — Foto: Reprodução/TV Globo/Fantástico

O rio Trichuli transbordou de forma violenta e arrastou estruturas inteiras. No centro da cidade, o bazar, onde havia muitas pessoas no momento da enchurrada, foi destruído.

Casas ficaram cobertas de lama. A água chegou a uma altura próxima do terceiro andar do banco da cidade.

Uma das principais ligações da cidade foi perdida. Um morador contou que atravessou a ponte cerca de 15 minutos antes de ela ser levada pela enchurrada. A família dele ficou do outro lado.

Sem a ponte, ele não conseguia encontrar os parentes nem voltar para casa. Por isso, permaneceu no centro da cidade em busca de notícias.

Enchente no Nepal. — Foto: Reprodução/TV Globo

A falta de eletricidade, telefone e internet dificultou a comunicação sobre as pessoas desaparecidas.

Na base do Exército do Nepal, familiares foram procurar informações. Uma lista com os nomes dos resgatados era consultada por quem tentava localizar parentes.

Um homem, que levou uma fotografia do irmão para tentar encontrá-lo, disse ter visto em um vídeo o carro do familiar, e buscava informações sobre o que havia acontecido. Em um hospital, familiares também aguardavam notícias.

Uma mulher contou que o tio estava desaparecido. Ele era motorista e estava em uma das áreas mais afetadas quando a tragédia aconteceu. Ela disse manter a esperança de encontrá-lo vivo porque ainda não havia comunicação com a região.

Felipe Pessanha mostra prédio de banco em cidade devastada por mar de lama. Água chegou ao terceiro andar. — Foto: Reprodução/TV Globo/Fantástico

Sobreviventes são retirados de áreas atingidas

Equipes de resgate encontraram pessoas em regiões remotas e em túneis em construção.

Uma mãe com um bebê pequeno foi retirada de uma das áreas próximas à fronteira com o Tibete. Um jovem aparentemente ferido também foi levado para atendimento médico.

Um motorista que trabalhava em uma hidrelétrica contou que dirigia um caminhão que transportava 15 funcionários quando ficou preso dentro de um túnel.

Ele conseguiu sair do veículo e nadar até uma área coberta pela lama. Segundo seu relato, acredita que os demais trabalhadores da hidrelétrica tenham morrido por causa da força dos rios.

Outro sobrevivente, de 84 anos, contou que teve a casa completamente destruída. Ele e outras pessoas conseguiram correr para uma montanha e passaram a noite no local até serem resgatados.

Entre os sobreviventes também estão uma menina de 6 anos, retirada dos escombros dois dias depois da avalanche, e uma mulher de 97 anos, que ficou coberta de lama e foi resgatada após nove horas.

O bisneto da idosa acompanhou o resgate.

“Eu fiquei muito emocionado quando tiraram ela de lá. Não sabia o que fazer, nem sei pôr em palavras”, contou.

A tragédia aconteceu durante um grande feriado sagrado para os hindus, período em que havia muitas pessoas em peregrinação nas montanhas.

Um jornalista nepalês que chegou às áreas atingidas antes mesmo do resgate disse nunca ter visto uma destruição daquela proporção.

“Eu cubro desastres desse tipo há uns 10 anos, mas nunca vi uma devastação tão grande. Não consigo colocar em palavras o que ouvi esses dias”, afirmou.

articles.title: Parque Shopping Prudente tem 4 dias de ofertas na 'Liquida da Independência' | G1
articles.standfirst: Campanha chega à 37ª edição com descontos de até 80% em mais de 50 lojas participantes, de 4 a 7 de setembro.
articles.summary: Campanha chega à 37ª edição com descontos de até 80% em mais de 50 lojas participantes, de 4 a 7 de setembro.
articles.body:
Descontos de até 80% são destaque no “Liquida da Independência” do Parque Shopping Prudente — Foto: Parque Shopping Prudente/Divulgação

O Parque Shopping Prudente prepara um verdadeiro show de ofertas para o feriado da Independência. Entre os dias 4 e 7 de setembro , o centro de compras realiza a 37ª edição do Liquida Parque , que neste ano ganha um novo formato: pela primeira vez, a campanha terá quatro dias de duração , acompanhando o feriado nacional de 7 de setembro.

Com a participação de mais de 50 lojas , o ‘ Liquida da Independência ’ reúne oportunidades em diferentes segmentos, com descontos de até 80% . Os clientes poderão encontrar produtos em promoção nas áreas de moda feminina, masculina e infantil, calçados, acessórios, beleza, eletrônicos, artigos para casa e supermercado.

A campanha também se estende à Praça de Alimentação , que reúne opções em promoção para diferentes gostos, incluindo pratos, porções, lanches, bebidas e sobremesas.

“O Liquida da Independência chega com uma novidade importante neste ano: serão quatro dias de campanha, aproveitando também o feriado de 7 de setembro. Preparamos uma seleção de ofertas em mais de 50 lojas, com descontos de até 80%, para que nossos clientes possam aproveitar ainda mais as oportunidades e encontrar produtos e serviços para diferentes necessidades em um único lugar”, destaca Daniel Alvarez, analista de Marketing do Parque Shopping Prudente.

Para quem já quer se programar, o folheto digital com as ofertas está disponível no site do shopping . Durante os quatro dias de campanha, os clientes também poderão acompanhar as principais oportunidades e novidades pelas redes sociais do centro de compras .

Alimentação: Açaí do Barão, All Chicken, Chiquinho Sorvetes, FitLand, Grão Real Café, KFC, McDonald’s, MilkyMoo, Mundo das Festas, Pasteloko, Roasted Potato, Sra. Massa, Suco Bagaço, Vó Laura Expresso, Woods Hamburgueria e YakiSushi.

Moda: Anticorpus, B1, Brandili, Donna Donna, Don Victor, Hering, Hombre, Martinna Clothing, Mar.B Basic, Nanes Moda Fitness e Nogueira Western.

Calçados: Arezzo, Chinelaria Parque, Pé Quente e World Tennis.

Acessórios: Chilli Beans, Edubolsas, Instituto Visão Solidária, Lua de Prata, Ryu Semijoias e Seiko.

Beleza: Espaço Laser, HairFit, L’Occitane Au Brésil, Melancita, Natura, O Boticário e Touti.

O Parque Shopping Prudente está localizado na Rua Siqueira Campos, 1545. Durante o Liquida da Independência, o funcionamento seguirá conforme abaixo:

Lojas : das 12h às 18h (com permanência facultativa até as 20h)

articles.title: No roofs, no toilets, no teachers: TOI check finds minuses in Rajasthan govt schools
articles.summary: India News: TOI reporters visited govt schools across six Rajasthan districts after the row over CJP volunteers inspecting campuses. What they found, from Kota’s .
articles.body: TOI reporters visited govt schools across six Rajasthan districts after the row over CJP volunteers inspecting campuses. What they found, from Kota’s coaching hub to desert villages and tragedy-hit Piplodi, was a system in which children study under tin sheds, squeeze into unsafe rooms, and sometimes find their school locked.In Kota, a primary school with 78 students operates from municipal parking kiosks and tin sheds. Three teachers run the school on deputation, with no permanent teaching posts sanctioned. A PWD survey found 61 school buildings in the district ruined and hundreds of classrooms unsafe.Across Barmer, Jaisalmer and Balotra, some schools lack buildings, while transfers have left senior-secondary streams without teachers. In Piplodi, Jhalawar, where a roof collapse killed seven children in July 2025, classes still run from a farmer’s two-room home as construction of a new school drags on.In the CM’s Sanganer constituency, 404 students at one school have been pushed into four rooms after a second building was declared unsafe.Assembly data shows 611 govt schools have no building of their own; 2,047 lack toilets; and 1,049 lack drinking water. Another 3,768 buildings and 83,783 classrooms are classified as completely dilapidated. Rajasthan also has 7,200 single-teacher schools and 1.5 lakh vacant teacher posts.It has 78 enrolled students from classes I-V who study in six classrooms but there can be no building inspection at Govt Primary School on MBS Road in Kota. The school, established in 2023, doesn’t have one.Children who come to study here gather under small tin sheds created next to municipal parking ticket kiosks. Pathways to success that all of India chases are all around them. But it’ll take a miracle for anyone in this batch to one day make that short walk to one of the city’s many fabled coaching centres, where many of India’s brightest prospects in medical and engineering come to hone their skills in a widely publicised ‘topper-producing’ machinery.Kota’s higher education success, riding entirely on private enterprise, hasn’t pulled up with it the city’s own govt education system. It’s a constituency that Rajasthan’s education minister Madan Dilawar represents, but that too has made little difference to many children who have been going to ‘school’ on footpaths, cramming into single rented rooms or under tin sheds in a state that sees extreme temperatures.Last week, a Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) delegation led by Ashutosh Ranka was chased away by a mob after it went on an inspection of a govt school in Jaipur. In Kota, though, there’s little that’s hidden behind walls about the state of primary schools. Within a day after this non-inspection, however, Rajasthan’s BJP govt led by CM Bhajan Lal Sharma pledged to spend Rs 12,000 crore on schools over three years.Shobana Gupta, the in-charge of the primary school on MBS Road in Ward 33, says, “We operate out of six municipal kiosks and from under a tin shade. We have adequate arrangements for drinking water, electricity, and basic toilet facilities available onsite. There are no sanctioned permanent teaching posts here yet. Three teachers are currently deployed on deputation to manage the classes.”At Govt Senior Secondary School in Vigyan Nagar — a designated centre for JEE and NEET — the school sits inside a Rajasthan Housing Board building that is falling apart. Nine classrooms need major repair. Two are unusable but funds haven’t been allocated yet for demolition or repairs. Mold has eaten into walls of functional classrooms and the school’s ‘smart classroom’. A part of the perimeter wall has given way. Thieves have stolen the school’s water taps and CCTV cameras worth Rs 70,000. Principal Anita Sharma is still waiting for funds.At Shiv Nagar, Govt Primary Sanskrit School has been running for eight years now out of a single rented room, reached by a muddy track that’s impassable in the rains. Enrolment has fallen to 8-10 students under one teacher in a locality of around 60,000 people.“This locality has children who want to study Sanskrit. I have repeatedly submitted memorandums, but no permanent building has been sanctioned yet,” said former ward councillor Dhanraj Gurjar Chechi.Dilawar, incidentally, publicly champions Sanskrit learning as part of Indian cultural values.At Govt Upper Primary School in Devripunia, Dharmpura — in Ladpura constituency of BJP MLA Kalpna Devi, roughly 10 km from Dilawar’s residence — 130-plus enrolled students share three classrooms built decades ago under Rajiv Gandhi Swarn Jyanti Pathshala scheme. The school was upgraded to upper-primary status in 2021, but the promised classroom expansion never came.On full-attendance days, children sit under trees, on the veranda, or on open ground. Drinking water comes via a temporary line from an adjoining field. Principal Chandra Prakash Meena has written to both the MLA and the minister. Days before this report, 27 students fell ill after eating their mid-day meal.A Public Works Department survey of Kota district’s 1,088 govt schools found 61 buildings entirely ruined and marked for demolition, plus two classrooms flagged as unsafe in each of 318 school buildings, and one classroom each in a further 98. Only 41 full buildings and 29 partial structures have been demolished so far.District collector Peeyush Samaria’s office has no record of any personal inspection visit to a govt school. Samaria remained unavailable for comment. Sanganer, Jaipur: The CM’s constituencyAt Bojyawas Govt Primary School, there are toilets, but they have no water. The water tank has cracked and dense cobwebs, indicating it hasn’t been in use for some time. The school shares space with a sub-health centre, where fungus covers medicine boxes and water stains mark chairs and registers.A staff member said open defecation has become routine for her. She does her best by consciously holding off the urge to use a toilet. The school itself has 10 students in classes 1 to 5 under a single teacher.Govt Secondary School, Kalyanpura, looks well-kept from the gate, till you learn that one of its two buildings has been shut as unsafe, leaving 404 students across classes 1–12 to squeeze into four rooms.The school runs two shifts, 7am–12 noon and 12:30–6pm, and some second-shift students sit under a tin shed outside because the classes can’t accommodate them. Washrooms don’t have regular water supply and are cleaned only twice a month, said a Class 12 student.With no security guard and a broken, low boundary wall, the campus has seen repeated thefts. As a result, each classroom door has three latches and three separate locks.At Govt Upper Primary Sanskrit School in Hasampur Basdi, 85 students from classes 1 to VIII are taught in four classrooms — one of which is assigned to a booth level officer for special intensive revision (SIR) work.Teacher Rajendra Verma produced letters he has submitted seeking a playground, boundary fencing and a tubewell. The school has been running on tanker water for close to a year, he said.At Govt Primary School in Hasampura, there was no need to interview anyone about the school’s condition. The gate was locked at 9.30am on a weekday. Former ward councillor Ram Singh Choudhary said he has been writing to govt for three years about the school’s lack of facilities. Jaisalmer & Barmer: Studying under treesIn Rajasthan’s desert border districts, several schools have no building.In Ramsar panchayat, Barmer, Govt Upper Primary School Azad Nagar was sanctioned in the 2022–23 budget and began classes in March 2023. But its 37 students study in a hut built by villagers or under trees.“Whether it rains, there is a storm or it is extremely hot, we have to study under trees,” said a Class V student.Land for the school was allotted only in 2024, and construction funds await sanction.At the Govt Higher Secondary School in Majal village, Samdari block (Balotra district), students and parents locked the school gate after nine teachers were transferred out at once, leaving senior secondary arts, science and agriculture streams without lecturers.“When there are no lecturers in the school, how will we study? How can Grade-II teachers perform the duties of lecturers?” a student asked.The protest ended after education officials agreed to post three teachers on deputation.Assembly data, drawn from UDISE 2025-26 figures, shows both districts have building-less schools: 36 in Barmer and 25 in Jaisalmer. Jaisalmer also features among districts hit hardest by a separate supply failure — a shortfall in the milk powder needed for the state’s Pannadhay Bal Gopal Yojana. Jhalawar: After 7 deaths, wait on for a new buildingOn the morning of July 25, 2025, the roof of Govt Upper Primary School in Piplodi, a tribal village in Jhalawar, collapsed during class hours. Seven children died; 21 were injured.A year on, Piplodi has visibly changed — better roads, more power connections, regular health camps, rising enrolment — but the one thing it still lacks is a functioning school building.Classes at the school have run since last August out of the two-room house of Mor Singh, a 60-year-old farmer and shepherd who vacated his own home so children would not lose another year of school.A new school building — eight classrooms, an anganwadi centre and a kitchen — is under construction, originally due by July 24, 2026. It has since been delayed after villagers raised concerns about construction quality when work began last November. Officials demolished the substandard work and restarted.“Construction of the school is taking longer than expected as villagers raised concerns about the quality of construction,” said Jhalawar collector Ajay Singh, adding that surprise inspections are now held every few weeks and the building should be ready by October.Among Rajasthan’s blocks, Jhalawar has the highest concentration of building-less govt schools. District-wide, 81 schools lack toilets.Assembly data show 611 govt schools statewide with no building of their own, including 10 girls’ schools, 2,047 schools with buildings that lack toilets, and 1,049 that lack drinking water. It’s not that govt doesn’t spend on educationRajasthan’s 2026–27 budget allocates Rs 64,205 crore to school and college education. Of this allocation, around 75% goes into staff salaries and only 10–15% goes infrastructure.The state employs the second-highest number of teachers in the country, at 7.93 lakh, second only to UP. Yet, it has 7,200 single-teacher govt schools serving over 1.5 lakh students. Around 1.5 lakh sanctioned teacher posts remain vacant.The state’s own infrastructure data lays out the scale of the problem: 3,768 school buildings, 83,783 classrooms and 16,765 toilets are classified as entirely dilapidated while another 2,19,902 classrooms and 29,753 toilets need repair.Over the past two years, govt says it has spent Rs 2,723 crore building 179 new school buildings and 7,945 new classrooms to replace dilapidated ones.With govt funds in scarce supply, state-run schools increasingly lean on voluntary and community money. Statewide, philanthropic donations for school development totalled Rs 138 crore in 2024 and Rs 140 crore in 2025.In Pali district, a donor-led ‘Aao Gaon Chalen’ campaign — connecting migrants and philanthropists to their native villages — has targeted raising Rs 300 crore for infrastructure work.“There are around 23,000 such teachers in the state who are posted in a school where they are not needed, and their posting should be in another school, but they have not accepted their new posting. For instance, in an English-medium school, a Hindi-medium teacher who was earlier posted does not accept their new posting after a transfer, and the Hindi medium school, where the teacher is needed, students are suffering in that school,” said Mahendra Pandey, chief general secretary of Rajasthan Primary and Secondary Teachers Association. Gen Z, Gen alpha protestsThe consequences have spilled onto the streets.In Sikar, Class 12 students protested dilapidated buildings that force school closures every time it rains, alongside a shortage of subject teachers.In Gangapur City (Sawai Madhopur), girls locked the gates of the Mahatma Gandhi English Medium School in Meena Badoda, Wazirpur, after the principal was pulled onto local-body election duty, compounding an existing teacher shortage.At Govt Senior Secondary School in Majal village in Balotra district, students locked the gates after nine teachers were transferred simultaneously.A Class XII student at Govt Higher Secondary School at Majal in Balotra said: “If we had to study without teachers, then we could have studied at home. What is the need to come to school? If a school is operational, teachers must be posted.”The infrastructure debate has become an open political fight.A civic campaign, ‘School Thik Karo’, backed by CJP, has sent volunteer teams to inspect schools across nine districts — Jaipur, Ajmer, Jodhpur, Udaipur, Dholpur, Bharatpur, Kota, Barmer and Hanumangarh — after receiving what it says are public requests.“It has been over a year since the school collapse tragedy in Jhalawar, and the education minister has still not shared a concrete plan on how over 80,000 classrooms in dilapidated conditions will be fixed. Students are being forced to study in unsafe buildings, risking their lives,” said CJP national spokesperson Ashutosh Ranka.One inspection, in Jaipur’s Bagru constituency, found a school that had been operating out of a buffalo shed for two and a half years after its own building was declared unsafe; it was shifted to a house only after drawing media attention.The state education department has now issued an order requiring prior permission for any outsider to enter school premises, and barring photography, videography, interviews or livestreaming involving students without the principal’s consent.Opposition leader Tikaram Jully called it an attempt to hide failures: “Instead of fixing schools, if you introduce ‘no entry’ measures just to hide your own failures, how can such accidents be prevented? A useless ‘double-engine’ govt,” Jully said.Additional reporting by Vimal Matta, Suparna Roy, Somdutt Trtpathi, Suntl Parmuwal & Shoeb KhanGet the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: Rain fury to continue across India: IMD warns of extremely heavy rain in these states; what travellers need to know
articles.summary: Several Indian regions will experience wet weather conditions through the first week of September. Heavy to very heavy rainfall is forecast across multiple states and eastern India. Odisha and Chhattisgarh face the highest rainfall threat with extremely heavy showers expected. Widespread rainfall will continue across northwest, central, and eastern India until September fifth. Northeast and southern regions will also see widespread and heavy rainfall during this period.
articles.body: Several parts of India are likely to remain under wet weather conditions through the first week of September, with the India Meteorological Department (IMD) forecasting heavy to very heavy rainfall across multiple states and isolated extremely heavy rainfall in parts of eastern and central India.According to the IMD's All India Weather Summary and Forecast Bulletin issued on August 31, a well-marked low pressure area over Gangetic West Bengal and adjoining areas of north coastal Odisha and northwest Bay of Bengal persisted on Monday morning. The system, accompanied by a cyclonic circulation extending up to 7.6 km above mean sea level, is likely to move west-northwestwards across north Odisha and Gangetic West Bengal during the next 24 hours.Odisha, Chhattisgarh under highest rainfall threatFor August 31, the IMD has forecast heavy to very heavy rainfall with isolated extremely heavy rainfall over Chhattisgarh and Odisha. Heavy to very heavy rainfall is also likely at isolated places in Arunachal Pradesh, Bihar, East Madhya Pradesh, East Uttar Pradesh, Jharkhand, Nagaland, Manipur, Mizoram and Tripura, as well as Uttarakhand.The weather department has also warned of heavy rainfall in Assam and Meghalaya, Himachal Pradesh, Jammu and Kashmir, Ladakh, West Bengal and Sikkim, and West Uttar Pradesh.Odisha is expected to see isolated extremely heavy rainfall again on September 1, while Chhattisgarh is forecast to receive heavy to very heavy rain. East Madhya Pradesh and Uttarakhand are also likely to experience heavy to very heavy rainfall.Rain to persist into SeptemberThe wet spell is not expected to end immediately. The IMD forecasts fairly widespread to widespread rainfall across several regions through September 5.In northwest India, Himachal Pradesh and Uttarakhand are expected to receive fairly widespread to widespread rain through September 5, while East Uttar Pradesh is likely to see similar conditions from September 1 to 5. Jammu and Kashmir and Ladakh are expected to remain wet through September 2.Central India is also likely to remain active. Chhattisgarh, East Madhya Pradesh and Vidarbha are forecast to receive fairly widespread to widespread rainfall through September 5, while West Madhya Pradesh is expected to see widespread rainfall from September 2 to 5.Across eastern India, widespread rainfall is forecast over Gangetic West Bengal, Sub-Himalayan West Bengal and Sikkim, and the Andaman and Nicobar Islands through September 5. Jharkhand and Odisha are likely to see widespread rain through September 2, while Bihar is expected to remain wet through September 2.Northeast and south also likely to see rainNortheast India is expected to remain under widespread rainfall during August 31-September 5. The IMD has forecast heavy rainfall over Assam and Meghalaya through this period, with Arunachal Pradesh likely to receive heavy rain from September 1 to 5. articles.title: Jaya Bachchan gave up her career for her children: The emotional truth about sacrifice, guilt and why loving your kids should never mean losing yourself
articles.summary: When Karan Johar once asked Jaya Bachchan why she walked away from acting at the peak of her career, her answer was far from simple. She shared that A.
articles.body: When Karan Johar once asked Jaya Bachchan why she walked away from acting at the peak of her career, her answer was far from simple. She shared that Amitabh Bachchan had once told her he didn't want a wife who worked fixed office hours. As his own career grew busier, Jaya felt someone needed to be around for their children full-time. She even remembered a moment when her daughter Shweta asked her not to leave for a shoot and to let her father go instead, a memory she described as painful. This conversation, from a 2007 episode of Koffee With Karan, still resonates with many parents today because the struggle she described hasn't gone away. It has simply taken new forms.The guilt that never really leavesModern parents, no matter what choice they make, often end up carrying some form of guilt. Working mothers can feel torn between being present at home and being present at work. Fathers today often want to be hands-on parents while still being expected to provide financially. Even parents who choose to stay home aren't spared. According to psychotherapist and relationship coach Delnna Rrajesh, a stay-at-home parent can genuinely love their children and still miss parts of the life they had before, and that doesn't make their love any less real.Loving your child and missing your old life can both be trueDelnna explains that emotional maturity means being able to hold two feelings at once. A mother who misses her career isn't loving her child less. A father who wishes for more professional freedom isn't regretting fatherhood. A caregiver who feels tired isn't resenting the person they care for. The problem, she says, starts when parents feel they aren't "allowed" to feel this way, because those buried emotions don't just disappear. They often turn into guilt, irritation or quiet resentment instead.Why the way you talk about sacrifice mattersAccording to Delnna, there's a big difference between saying "I gave this up because of you" and saying "I made the best decision I could at that time." The first puts the emotional weight on the child. The second keeps the responsibility with the adult, where it belongs. Every family will go through phases where one person sacrifices more, whether it's sleep, career growth or personal time. That isn't unhealthy on its own. What becomes harmful is when that sacrifice is quietly kept as a debt to be repaid later. Delnna points out that children absorb far more from watching their parents than from any lecture. A daughter who sees her mother chase her own goals learns something valuable about self-worth. A son who watches his father take on cooking and caregiving learns a broader idea of what it means to be a man.It shouldn't always be the mother's turn to sacrificeOne of the more important points Delnna raises is how caregiving decisions are almost always framed around the mother first. Instead of asking whether the mother should keep working, families would benefit more from asking how work, money and childcare responsibilities can be shared between both partners. Sometimes stepping back makes sense for the mother, sometimes for the father, and sometimes both partners simply cut back a little. There is no one right formula, and no version of parenting is automatically more devoted or more ambitious than another.Questions every couple should ask before making a big sacrificeBefore one partner gives up something significant for the family, Delnna suggests asking a few honest questions. Is this choice being made freely, or out of fear of disappointing someone? What is being gained, and what is being quietly grieved? Is this sacrifice meant to be temporary or permanent? And most importantly, when will the arrangement be revisited? Love, as Delnna puts it, may sometimes ask people to give things up. But it should never ask anyone to completely lose themselves in the process.Looking for trusted parenting advice? Commercial models span credits for creators, seat-based SaaS for studios and brands, and enterprise licensing with API access.In a press release, the company stated that SparkStation rolls out in three phases: beta access (August 29), general availability (October 1), and enterprise API tier (November 1). articles.title: A New Orleans couple found a 1,900-year-old Roman sailor’s gravestone buried in their backyard; it had vanished from an Italian museum during WWII and has now returned home
articles.summary: US News: Sometimes, a normal backyard hides a piece of history that has traveled further than anyone could ever imagine. A report published by Tulane Universit.
articles.body: Sometimes, a normal backyard hides a piece of history that has traveled further than anyone could ever imagine. A report published by Tulane University state that a couple in New Orleans recently unearthed a marble gravestone beneath their property that was almost 2,000 years old and absent from an Italian museum since the chaos of World War II. Now, the incredible find has come full circle, with the ancient Roman artifact being returned to the Italian city where it was first discovered. Scroll down to read the details.A Roman tombstone, lurking in New OrleansAccording to the University website, the marble tablet, dating from the second century A.D., commemorates Sextus Congenius Verus, a sailor who served in the Praetorian fleet based at Misenum near Naples. It was first discovered in 1866 near the old Roman port city of Centumcellae, today called Civitavecchia. It then passed into the collection of the city’s civic museum. But the story took a turn during the Second World War. The gravestone was lost from the collection and the museum was destroyed. For decades scholars had thought the ancient monument was lost forever until March 2025 and was then found in the backyard. The stone was found by anthropologist Daniella Santoro, of Tulane University, and her husband, Aaron Lorenz, as they worked in the backyard of their home in New Orleans. They took note of the odd slab because it had Latin inscriptions. Santoro contacted Susann S. Lusnia, a professor of classical studies at Tulane University, to see if she could help identify it.Lusnia immediately recognized the lettering and language to be consistent with an authentic Roman funerary inscription. She started searching scholarly databases with words from the inscription. The research soon produced a surprising result: the stone seemed to be the same monument that had been documented in Civitavecchia before vanishing in the Second World War.The archeological mystery unveiledIt was a remarkable moment of identification for Lusnia. The inscription was more than an ancient Roman object. It was a known object, with a known history, so it was possible to follow its path from Roman antiquity to an Italian museum and finally to an American backyard. Once the connection was established, Lusnia reached out to colleagues in Italy, and helped to set up communications with the National Archeological Museum of Civitavecchia. The find quickly grabbed international attention as historians, archeologists and the public became intrigued by the mystery of how a nearly 1,900-year-old Roman monument had come to New Orleans.Taking it home through international collaborationThe final return of the artifact involved a number of organizations on both sides of the Atlantic. The FBI Art Crime Team collaborated with the Consulate General of Italy in New York, the Italian Carabinieri Command for the Protection of Cultural Heritage, and Italian judicial authorities. The owners have agreed to return the tablet to Italy voluntarily. The ancient gravestone was returned in April 2026, according to the required procedures. The artifact has been cleaned and returned to the collection from which it was missing for more than 80 years.An old story, a new chapterThe gravestone is being prepared for public exhibition at the National Archeological Museum of Civitavecchia. It will be one of the featured artifacts when the museum reopens September 18 after a massive renovation. The new museum will display archeological artifacts, multimedia presentations and interactive exhibits that illustrate more than 3,000 years of Civitavecchia’s history. The importance of the return of the tablet is not only for its age, but for the return of a key element of the city’s archeological heritage. For Lusnia, the journey is a powerful reminder that history can emerge in the most unexpected of places. An artifact missing since 1943 survived generations intact before turning up thousands of miles away, waiting to be recognized. A Roman sailor’s gravestone has come home, as a reminder that even after almost 2,000 years and decades of being lost, the past can find its way back.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.body: NEW DELHI: Prime Minister Narendra Modi on Monday paid floral tribute to Mahatma Gandhi at his memorial in Bishkek and interacted with members of Indian and Kyrgyz communities ahead of the 26th Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO) Summit.PM Modi paid his respects at the Mahatma Gandhi memorial before participating in the SCO Summit in the Kyrgyz capital. For us, to have the opportunity to share the same stage with these great maestros and outstanding personalities was an immense joy and we really believe that this can open up new opportunities for our future events, to increase this marvelous and beautiful collaboration between our associations and our cultures."Jyldyz Kuvatova, founder of the Art of Living Foundation in Kyrgyzstan and professor at the American University of Central Asia, said, "We're so excited to be here. It was so intense, but it's so much worth it. And we had a performance, we're very excited and thank you for inviting us."Hatha yoga instructor Arina Niiazbekova, who is also associated with classical theatre, ballet and Indian classical dance, said the workshops provided an opportunity to learn from renowned gurus and performers."I work in the theatre, classical theatre, and I am ballet soloist, teacher, choreographer and the leader of the classical group. It was just like a dream coming true," he said.PM Modi in Bishkek for SCO SummitAccording to the Ministry of External Affairs, PM Modi has arrived in Bishkek to participate in the 26th SCO Leadership Summit, which brings together 10 member states, 15 partner countries and two observer countries for discussions on regional and global issues.PM Modi is also scheduled to hold bilateral meetings on the sidelines of the summit, including with Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian and Russian President Vladimir Putin.His visit to Bishkek is the second leg of his two-country tour following his State Visit to Uzbekistan, where he held talks with Uzbek President Shavkat Mirziyoyev.During the Uzbekistan visit, India and Uzbekistan elevated their ties to a Comprehensive Strategic Partnership and agreed to expand cooperation in areas including trade, investment, infrastructure, digital public infrastructure, artificial intelligence, critical minerals, energy, space, agriculture, healthcare, pharmaceuticals, education and culture.The two sides also set a target of increasing bilateral trade to USD 5 billion by 2030.Before leaving Tashkent, PM Modi thanked President Mirziyoyev for his hospitality, saying, "Thank you, Uzbekistan! articles.summary: US News: US President Donald Trump said on Sunday that Iran's Kharg Island was being “blown to smithereens”, without providing details, as tensions between Was.
articles.body: US President Donald Trump said on Sunday that Iran's Kharg Island was being “blown to smithereens”, without providing details, as tensions between Washington and Tehran escalated after the first known US strikes on Iran in weeks.Kharg Island is a major Iranian energy hub that handled about 90% of the country's oil exports before the war began with US and Israeli attacks on February 28. Any significant damage to the island could disrupt Iran's oil trade and place further pressure on its economy."Kharg Island being blown to smithereens!!! President DJT," Trump said on social media.The White House and US Defense Department did not immediately respond to Reuters requests for comment. Reuters also verified that an accompanying video showing dramatic explosions had been artificially generated.The U.S. strikes earlier hit two Iranian rocket launchers on Larak Island in the Strait of Hormuz. U.S. Central Command said it had taken "limited, precise" action against Iranian Revolutionary Guard minelaying forces that posed an "imminent threat" in the strategic waterway.The command did not provide further details.Iran subsequently launched ballistic missiles towards two U.S. bases in Jordan, Iranian media reported. Jordan's armed forces said they had intercepted eight missiles that entered its airspace.A Fox News reporter, citing a U.S. source, said nearly all incoming missiles "have been intercepted at this point", indicating limited immediate impact.Iran's Revolutionary Guards said the attack killed and wounded several soldiers and civilians and vowed a "response and punishment" from Tehran, according to Iranian state media.Strait of Hormuz faces renewed disruptionThe escalation has also raised fresh concerns over shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, a critical route for global energy supplies.The number of visible commodity vessels crossing the waterway fell to about five a day over the weekend, according to shipping data. The actual number could be higher because some vessels have switched off their automatic identification systems to avoid potential attacks.Trump said last week that all mines in the international waters of the strait had either been detonated or removed, and warned Iran that any vessel laying new mines would be destroyed.While Trump has repeatedly said the waterway remains open, Iran's Revolutionary Guards' navy has rejected that claim as "an obvious lie", saying the strait remains closed to ships without Iranian permission.The Strait of Hormuz carried nearly one-fifth of global crude oil and liquefied natural gas shipments before it was blockaded during the six-month-old Iran war.Iran is the third-largest producer in the Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Delhi court sentences conman Sukesh Chandrasekhar to 8-year jail term for impersonating SC judge
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: A Delhi court sentenced conman Sukesh Chandrasekhar to eight years of rigorous imprisonment for impersonating a Supreme Court judge and att.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: A Delhi court sentenced conman Sukesh Chandrasekhar to eight years of rigorous imprisonment for impersonating a Supreme Court judge and attempting to influence a bail proceeding in another criminal case.Chief judicial magistrate Harshita Mishra of Tis Hazari courts sentenced Chandrasekhar to two years' rigorous imprisonment and fined him Rs 5,000 under IPC Section 170, two years' rigorous imprisonment and fined him Rs 5,000 under Section 189, and four years' rigorous imprisonment under Section 507.In an order dated August 29, which was made available on Sunday, the court said, "The sentence must reflect that the criminal justice system distinguishes between an isolated unlawful act and a deliberate sequence of acts designed to manipulate, intimidate or interfere with the lawful functioning of public institutions."The court directed that all three substantive sentences would run consecutively, taking the total jail term to eight years. In case of default in payment of the fines, Chandrasekhar will undergo an additional month's imprisonment.The court had on August 20 convicted Chandrasekhar under sections 170, 189 and 507 of the IPC, dealing with impersonation and threat.According to the sentencing order, Chandrasekhar made multiple calls on April 28, 2017, to judicial officer Poonam Choudhary while impersonating a Supreme Court judge from South India and using a regional accent to make the impersonation appear credible.The court said the objective was to influence a judicial proceeding concerning Chandrasekhar's liberty in another criminal case, describing the conduct as an attack on the sanctity and integrity of the judicial process."The choice of the person impersonated was therefore not accidental," the court said, observing that Chandrasekhar deliberately sought to appropriate the credibility attached to a constitutional post.The court rejected the argument that his failure to deceive the judicial officer or secure bail should be treated as a mitigating circumstance, saying the unsuccessful attempt did not make the act of impersonation innocuous.It also noted that Chandrasekhar did not demonstrate genuine remorse or contrition during the trial and instead questioned the credibility of the complainant judicial officer.The court said the case was particularly concerning in the present technological environment, where deepfakes, AI-generated audio-visual material, cloned voices and spoofed communications could make impersonation of constitutional authorities increasingly sophisticated."The sentence in the present case must necessarily carry a deterrent message," the court said, stressing the need to protect public confidence in the justice system.The court also considered a list of criminal cases pending against Chandrasekhar but said those cases, being sub judice and not resulting in convictions, could not be taken into account while deciding his sentence.The court directed articles.body: IMPHAL: Two villagers were killed and another injured in a gun attack by suspected militants in Manipur's Kangpokpi district on Monday morning, officials told news agency PTI.According to a district official, armed men opened indiscriminate fire using sophisticated weapons in N Teikhang, a Kuki-inhabited village under T Waichong subdivision, killing two people and setting several houses on fire.The attack took place around 9.30 am, he said.The deceased were identified as Lamtinthang, 35, and Neichin.Another villager, 65-year-old Seilun, sustained bullet injuries in the attack.The firing forced several villagers to flee their homes and take shelter in the nearby forests, officials said.A heavy exchange of fire was underway between armed groups belonging to the two communities in the hill village, they said.Security forces were being rushed to the area to bring the situation under control.The attack came days after suspected militants ambushed a vehicle in the district, killing four Naga civilians and injuring another person.More than 20 people have been killed in separate firing incidents, while several houses have been burnt, since violence broke out between the Naga and Kuki communities in the state in February.(With agency inputs)Stay updated with the latest Imphal news. articles.title: In 2025, Texas engineers mixed 4.5 tons of recycled plastic into a highway, replacing part of the bitumen to test how it handles extreme heat
articles.summary: US News: On State Highway 205 in Rockwall, a suburb east of Dallas, engineers paved a 3,500-foot stretch of road using about 4.5 tons of recycled plastic mixed.
articles.body: On State Highway 205 in Rockwall, a suburb east of Dallas, engineers paved a 3,500-foot stretch of road using about 4.5 tons of recycled plastic mixed directly into the asphalt. The project, led by Sahadat Hossain, a civil engineering professor at the University of Texas at Arlington, replaces a portion of the petroleum-based bitumen that normally binds asphalt with melted plastic made from discarded bags, bottles and other everyday waste. After years of laboratory testing and smaller pavement trials, the May 2025 project brought the technology onto an active Texas highway. The team is now watching how the material performs under regular traffic, heavy vehicles and Texas heat. The idea is relatively simple: instead of sending difficult-to-recycle plastic to landfills or letting it escape into the environment, researchers want to give some of it another use while also reducing the amount of conventional petroleum-based binder needed to build roads.How researchers turn discarded plastic into road materialThe technology developed by Hossain's team is designed to change the composition of asphalt without requiring an entirely different type of road. Conventional asphalt is made from aggregates such as crushed stone and sand held together by bitumen, a sticky petroleum-based binder. In the Texas project, roughly 8% to 10% of the bitumen is replaced with recycled plastic. The plastic waste is first cleaned and shredded into small pieces before being introduced into the hot asphalt mixture. At high temperatures, the plastic melts and becomes incorporated into the material as the asphalt is produced. The approach is aimed at two problems at once. Plastic waste is notoriously difficult to manage, particularly when it comes from thin bags and other products that are not easily processed through standard recycling systems. At the same time, road engineers are constantly looking for ways to make asphalt last longer and withstand increasingly demanding conditions. Texas provides a particularly useful testing ground because pavement is exposed to intense summer heat as well as heavy traffic. When conventional bitumen becomes softer under high temperatures, roads can become more vulnerable to deformation, including the grooves and depressions known as rutting.Hossain's team had already spent years testing plastic-infused asphalt before taking the material onto State Highway 205. Laboratory experiments allowed researchers to examine the physical properties of different mixtures under controlled conditions, while smaller pavement trials provided an opportunity to see how the material behaved outside the lab. The Rockwall project represents a much more significant test because the road is being used normally rather than being reserved for research. Cars and trucks are passing over the material every day, while the pavement is exposed to the full range of weather conditions. That real-world exposure is important because a road can perform well in a controlled experiment and still behave differently once it is subjected to years of traffic, temperature changes and moisture. Researchers can now monitor the Rockwall section for cracking, rutting and other forms of deterioration. The results should provide a clearer picture of whether recycled plastic can remain stable inside asphalt over a long period and whether the material offers any practical advantage over conventional road construction.Why Texas is testing plastic in highwaysThe project comes at a time when plastic waste has become a global environmental problem. More than 400 million tons of plastic are produced around the world each year, but less than 10% is recycled. The remainder can end up in landfills, be incinerated or enter rivers, oceans and other parts of the environment. While recycling rates vary considerably depending on the type of plastic and the country where it is collected, many everyday plastic products have limited value in existing recycling systems. That is part of the reason researchers are interested in finding uses that do not depend entirely on traditional recycling. Instead of turning waste plastic back into another plastic product, the Texas approach incorporates it into infrastructure that could remain in service for years. A road therefore becomes a potential long-term destination for material that might otherwise have been thrown away. There is also a practical reason for looking at plastic as part of asphalt. Bitumen itself is derived from petroleum, and asphalt production and road construction require large quantities of it. Replacing even a relatively small portion of the binder with another material could reduce the amount of bitumen required for a road, although the environmental and economic benefits depend on how the plastic is sourced, processed and incorporated.The researchers are not presenting the technology as a complete answer to either plastic pollution or road deterioration. Instead, the Rockwall project is testing whether the two problems can be addressed together. If the modified asphalt performs well over time, it could create another outlet for certain types of waste plastic while giving transportation agencies another material option for pavement construction. There are still questions to answer. A road has to remain safe and structurally sound for years, and any new material used at highway scale has to meet demanding engineering requirements. Researchers also need to understand how the plastic behaves as the pavement ages and whether there are any environmental concerns associated with its long-term use. Those questions cannot be answered by a single paving project, which is why continued monitoring will be central to the research.What the Rockwall road could mean for future projectsThe 3,500-foot section of State Highway 205 is therefore best understood as a large-scale field experiment. The UTA team can now observe how its recycled-plastic asphalt responds to the conditions that matter most to transportation agencies: traffic, heat, weather and time. The road's performance will help researchers determine whether the laboratory results translate into a material that can be used reliably on public highways. The team has also discussed extending the work to other parts of Texas, including Fort Worth and Amarillo. Testing the material in different locations could be particularly useful because pavement conditions are not identical across the state. Traffic volumes, temperatures, weather patterns and soil conditions can all affect how a road ages. Comparing different sites would allow researchers to see whether the material's performance remains consistent outside Rockwall.For Hossain, the broader appeal of the technology lies in giving waste plastic a purpose beyond its short original lifespan. A plastic bag or bottle may be used for only minutes or days, but once incorporated into road infrastructure, the material could remain part of a working pavement for years. That does not eliminate the need to reduce plastic production, improve recycling or prevent waste from reaching the environment, but it does offer another possible route for dealing with some of the plastic that is already being discarded.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: 'No compelling circumstance': SC declines to intervene in CJP's September 5 protest march
articles.summary: India News: NEW DELHI: The Supreme Court on Monday declined to intervene against Cockroach Janata Party's protest march on September 5, saying that maintenance of.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: The Supreme Court on Monday declined to intervene against Cockroach Janata Party's protest march on September 5, saying that maintenance of law and order was primarily the responsibility of the government and police.A bench of Chief Justice of India Surya Kant and Justices Joymala Bagchi and V Mohana said that there is no reason to presume that the proposed demonstration would insult in any untoward incident."We will at least, as of now, presume everybody will behave in a peaceful manner. Right now there is no compelling circumstance to assume that any untoward thing will happen," the CJI observed.The bench issued notice to the Centre and Delhi Police and posted the next hearing for September 10, along with other matters concerning the student protests.This comes after a plea was filed by retired Delhi Police officer Rajendra Singh, seeking directions to ensure that large-scale demonstrations and protest marches in sensitive areas of the national capital are held only after obtaining requisite police permissions.The counsel, appearing for Singh, urged the apex court to hear the matter on September 3, citing the proposed march and the upcoming BRICS Summit in Delhi on September 12-13.The counsel referred to the violence during the July 20 Sansad March announced by the CJP and cautioned that another incident could occur, even if not directly attributable to the organisers.The CJI, however, said the court could not proceed on the assumption that something untoward would happen and reiterated that the police authorities were competent to deal with any law-and-order situation."Before us, there is no identified group. You please impress upon the Union or NCT Delhi. It's for them to maintain law and order. They should act as per law," the CJI said."They are expected to maintain law and order, and the enforcing agency has the responsibility to maintain law and order... We are expecting them to act within that framework. From both sides, we are expecting that they will respect, they will conduct themselves, and they will follow the law of the land...," he added.The CJP has announced the September 5 march in Delhi, alleging that the Centre failed to honour its commitment to withdraw cases against students who participated in the July protests over the alleged examination paper leakGet the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: In 1985, CNN founder Ted Turner bought thousands of acres in Florida; the former plantation became a major private wildlife landscape
articles.summary: US News: Ted Turner’s homes were never simply places to live. The CNN founder built a remarkable property portfolio that stretched across vast ranches, wildlif.
articles.body: Ted Turner’s homes were never simply places to live. The CNN founder built a remarkable property portfolio that stretched across vast ranches, wildlife landscapes and historic plantations covering roughly 2 million acres. Among the most interesting was ‘Avalon,’ a former cotton plantation near Tallahassee, Florida, that Turner bought in 1985 and gradually expanded into a much larger private landscape. Architectural Digest reported that the property had grown to about 25,000 acres by 2004, with a grand Colonial Revival house, gardens and lakes at its centre. Decades later, Avalon remains closely linked to Turner’s conservation vision. Tall Timbers reports how the estate was being managed with an eye on wildlife, habitat and its long-term future, revealing how Turner’s enormous land holdings became about more than ownership and careful stewardship of natural landscape.Why did Ted Turner buy Avalon in FloridaTurner purchased Avalon near Tallahassee in 1985. At the time, the property covered about 8,000 acres and had previously been a cotton plantation and wild quail hunting site. The name Avalon came from the legends surrounding King Arthur. As Architectural Digest reported, Turner initially considered calling it Camelot, but eventually chose Avalon because he felt it better suited what he considered a mystical place. The initial purchase was already substantial, but Turner did not stop there. By 2004, he had acquired surrounding land and increased the size of Avalon by another 25,000 acres. Turner explained that he bought more land because he wanted it and believed land was something that lasted. That expansion transformed Avalon from a large private property into a vast landscape where wildlife and land management became central to its identity.Importance of wildlife at AvalonAvalon has a long history as a quail hunting property, but its role extends well beyond recreation. The property is home to quail, turkey, deer and black bears. It also supports red-cockaded woodpeckers, a declining species that has established 18 active clusters on the property, according to Tall Timbers. Land conservation has also become a major part of Avalon’s future. More than 8,000 acres were placed under a conservation easement with The Nature Conservancy in 1988. In 2023, another 13,000-plus acres were placed into conservation through Florida Forever. These agreements prevent the land from being developed. Avalon was also being considered as a long-term home for gopher tortoises relocated from areas facing development. Tall Timbers reported that more than 5,000 acres could provide suitable soil and habitat for them.How is Avalon managed todayThe story of Avalon did not end with Turner’s purchase. Tall Timbers reports a new approach to managing the property under Karl Halbig, who arrived as its manager in August 2022. Halbig oversees more than 21,450 acres and initially resisted making immediate changes. Instead, he spent his first year learning how Avalon worked through different seasons and understanding how its various teams operated. As per Tall Timbers, he mapped the entire property using GPS, including roads, quail courses, food plots, feed trails and fields used by young birds. That information helped form a detailed management plan, giving the team a clearer way to measure whether changes were actually improving the land.Ted Turner’s Florida homeAt the heart of Avalon stood a 15,000-square-foot Colonial Revival house built in 1938, the same year Turner was born. The property also included gardens and several lakes, giving the home a distinctly different character from the enormous western ranches associated with Turner. Turner and actor Jane Fonda were married at Avalon in 1991. The couple later divorced in 2001, but the Florida property remained part of Turner’s wider land portfolio. As per Architectural Digest, he did not have a swimming pool at Avalon or at any of his other homes because he was simply not interested in pools. The detail offers a glimpse into the practical attitude that the surrounding land mattered more than conventional luxury features.Where did Ted Turner live later in his lifeTed Turner became one of America’s most prominent media figures, owning an extraordinary collection of properties across the United States and Argentina. According to Architectural Digest, his land holdings eventually reached across ranches in states including Montana, New Mexico, Nebraska, Colorado, Kansas and South Dakota, as well as properties in Argentina. His homes varied considerably. Some were working ranches, while others were historic estates or wildlife-focused properties. In his later years, Turner lived on one of his Montana ranches, where fishing remained one of his favourite activities. Yet Avalon in Florida stands out because of how dramatically Turner expanded it after buying the property.Avalon as one of Ted Turner’s lasting legacyTurner’s property empire was enormous, but Avalon illustrates why simply describing him as a major landowner misses part of the story. Across his ranches and estates, Turner increasingly connected land ownership with wildlife and conservation. At Avalon, that approach continues through careful habitat management, conservation agreements and efforts to protect species. Halbig described Avalon as deeply sentimental to Turner and saying that he wanted to protect the property for him. His goal was to leave the land in better condition for future generations. What began in 1985 with the purchase of an 8,000-acre former plantation grew into a landscape of more than 21,000 acres under active management. For Turner, the value of the property was not limited to the house at its centre. It was the land itself, and the wildlife and natural systems that depended on it.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: From garbage mountains to cleaner cities: How Delhi is showing India the way
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: For years, Delhi’s three giant landfill sites at Bhalswa, Okhla and Ghazipur have been hard to miss — both physically and as a reminder of .
articles.body: NEW DELHI: For years, Delhi’s three giant landfill sites at Bhalswa, Okhla and Ghazipur have been hard to miss — both physically and as a reminder of how badly the capital has struggled to deal with its waste.Now, there is finally some visible progress. Around 2.16 crore metric tonnes of legacy waste has been processed at the three sites and 100 acres of land reclaimed, according to the Delhi government.The numbers underline the scale of the exercise. Bhalswa has seen around 1.02 crore tonnes of waste processed and 45 acres reclaimed. At Okhla, 70 lakh tonnes have been processed and 35 acres recovered, while Ghazipur has accounted for another 44 lakh tonnes and 20 acres.Together, the reclaimed 100 acres is a sizeable piece of land in a city where every available acre is under pressure. The government has fixed December this year as the deadline for flattening Bhalswa and clearing Okhla, while Ghazipur has been given until December 2027.To put the scale into perspective, the roughly 1 crore metric tonnes of waste processed at Bhalswa alone translates to nearly 15 lakh truckloads of garbage.And the 100 acres of land reclaimed across the three sites is roughly equivalent to the area of nearly 60 international football fields. These comparisons underline just how enormous the clean-up exercise is — and how much urban land had effectively been locked up under mountains of waste.The harder part starts after the mountains disappearGetting rid of old waste is a major task, but it does not by itself solve Delhi’s garbage problem. The city continues to generate fresh waste every day, and some of it still reaches the landfill sites even as biomining is being carried out. That is why the latest deadlines will ultimately be judged not just by how much old waste is removed, but by whether Delhi can prevent new piles from building up again.There is reason to be cautious. Okhla, for instance, has already seen its deadline revised several times, with the target pushed back again this year. Delhi has therefore been here before — announcing timelines, beginning remediation and then having to extend the deadline. This time, the difference has to come from what happens alongside the clean-up. Unless waste generated today is processed properly, tomorrow’s legacy waste problem will simply begin taking shape.And this is not just Delhi’s problem. Across India, cities are facing the same difficult equation: more people, more construction, more consumption and consequently more waste. The Union govt said in January that nearly 25 crore metric tonnes of legacy waste had been identified across 2,488 large dumpsites. Of these, 1,138 dumpsites had been completely remediated, while work was under way at another 1,020. More than 15.51 crore tonnes had been processed and over 8,484 acres of land reclaimed. The scale shows why landfill remediation has become an urban land and infrastructure issue, not merely a sanitation exercise.India is generating waste faster than it can wish it awayThe bigger concern is what happens to the waste being generated now. India’s urban areas produce nearly 1.62 lakh tonnes of municipal solid waste every day. That volume is expected to rise sharply as cities expand, with annual waste generation projected at about 165 million tonnes by 2030 and 436 million tonnes by 2050.That changes the nature of the challenge. A city cannot permanently solve its waste problem by finding another plot of land, building a bigger landfill or periodically sending machines to mine old garbage. It has to ensure that a much larger share of what households, markets, offices and construction sites throw away is segregated, recycled, composted, recovered or processed before it reaches a landfill.Delhi’s lesson: Clean-up must become a systemDelhi is now trying to build that second layer into its strategy. The government says preparations have been completed for four new waste-to-energy plants, with the aim of creating enough capacity to process the waste generated every day. At Ghazipur, material recovered after processing is already being put to use for filling low-lying areas and preparing road bases. In other words, the idea is to extract value from the waste rather than simply move it from one place to another. “The Delhi government is focused on the scientific management of all kinds of waste,” chief minister Rekha Gupta said.That approach reflects a broader change in the way Indian cities are beginning to look at waste. Bengaluru, for instance, has been working on processing accumulated legacy waste at sites including Mandur and Bellahalli. Its 2025-26 civic budget identified nearly 97.82 lakh tonnes of accumulated legacy waste for processing at sites including Mandur and Bellahalli, with biomining and bioremediation forming part of the effort.The city has also had to tackle a more basic problem: waste that is simply dumped in the wrong place. In August, Bengaluru launched a ‘Freedom from Waste’ campaign aimed at clearing construction debris, legacy garbage, soil and dumping blackspots. That experience carries a simple message for Delhi. Sophisticated waste-processing plants cannot do the whole job if collection systems, segregation and enforcement remain weak.Other cities are grappling with the same questionThere is clearly interest in Delhi’s experience as well. In 2025, Karnataka chief minister DK Shivakumar visited Delhi along with Greater Bengaluru Authority officials to study the capital’s approach to urban planning and waste management. The delegation visited facilities including the Okhla landfill and Tehkhand waste-to-energy project. Bengaluru was looking at Delhi for ideas on how to deal with a problem that is increasingly common across large Indian cities.The global lesson: Stop making new garbage mountainsCities outside India offer another perspective. Seoul, for instance, once had an enormous waste problem of its own. Between 1978 and 1993, a river island was used as a dumping ground and accumulated around 92 million cubic metres of waste, creating two garbage mountains almost 98 metres high. Once dumping stopped, the site was sealed and eventually transformed into five ecological parks.Singapore has taken a different route, focusing heavily on reducing the amount of waste that ultimately needs to be landfilled. The city-state relies on incineration and waste-to-energy plants to cut the volume of waste requiring landfill disposal by as much as 90%. It also places increasing emphasis on reducing waste and improving recycling.The models are different, and Delhi cannot simply copy another city. But the underlying lesson is similar: a landfill should not be the end point of a city’s waste-management system. The less waste that reaches it, the less likely it is that another Bhalswa, Okhla or Ghazipur will emerge.Now comes the real testThe recovery of 100 acres is significant because land is one of the most valuable resources in a crowded capital. But the achievement will mean much more if the reclaimed sites remain free of another accumulation of waste.That is where Delhi’s experiment could become important for the rest of India. Biomining can deal with the waste of the past. New processing capacity can deal with much of the waste generated today. But neither will work on its own without segregation, recycling, reliable collection and enforcement.The real milestone, therefore, will not be the day the last visible garbage mountain disappears. It will be the day Delhi can generate millions of tonnes of waste without allowing another mountain to take its place. If the capital can make that transition, its reclaimed 100 acres will represent more than land recovered from garbage. articles.title: US treasury excludes several reporters from covering G20 finance meet
articles.summary: US News: The US Treasury Department has excluded journalists from several major news organisations, including The New York Times, Bloomberg News and The Wall S.
articles.body: The US Treasury Department has excluded journalists from several major news organisations, including The New York Times, Bloomberg News and The Wall Street Journal, from covering the G20 finance ministers' meeting in Asheville, North Carolina.The meeting, hosted by Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, is being held amid heightened global market volatility and the ongoing US-Iran conflict. The gathering brings together finance ministers, central bank governors and senior economic officials from the world's leading economies.The Treasury has not explained why it rejected the accreditation requests. Bessent told The Associated Press that the decision "has nothing to do with point of view".According to Bloomberg News, several of its journalists, including reporters based in the US, France, Italy, Japan and China, were denied access. The news agency said the exclusion undermines media freedom and public accountability.The New York Times also reported that its Treasury correspondent Alan Rappeport, who has covered the department and such international meetings since 2017, was denied credentials.However, Times Berlin bureau chief Jim Tankersley was allowed to attend after German officials intervened, Bloomberg reported.The Times condemned the decision, calling it an attempt by the Trump administration to undermine independent journalism and evade public scrutiny, particularly as issues including Iran, sanctions, inflation and global bond markets are on the G20 agenda.The Wall Street Journal also did not receive access, though the newspaper declined to comment, according to the reports.The US is holding the G20 presidency this year, with the Treasury expecting more than 200 journalists from dozens of countries to cover the finance ministers' meeting, which runs through Tuesday.The development comes amid broader tensions between the Trump administration and the US media, including restrictions imposed on journalists covering the Pentagon.Catch the latest World News and Live updates.
