articles.title: US sees major Javelin push in India as Tata, Raytheon and Lockheed Martin sign MoU
articles.summary: News News: Tata Advanced Systems Limited (TASL) and the Javelin Joint Venture (JJV), a partnership between Raytheon, an RTX business, and Lockheed Martin, have s.
articles.body: Tata Advanced Systems Limited (TASL) and the Javelin Joint Venture (JJV), a partnership between Raytheon, an RTX business, and Lockheed Martin, have signed a memorandum of understanding (MoU) to co-produce the Javelin All Up Round (AUR) in India.According to Lockheed Martin, TASL has been selected as the JJV's prime Indian partner for future in-country co-production. The two sides will explore setting up a facility in India for the final assembly and integration of the Javelin missile, along with production of some components.The agreement comes days after the Indian Army has finalised a Rs 292-crore government-to-government deal with the United States to acquire around 60 Javelin anti-tank guided missiles.The deal comes under the Army's sixth emergency procurement window and follows efforts to strengthen critical battlefield capabilities after Operation Sindoor.The Javelin is a man-portable, fire-and-forget, medium-range anti-tank missile designed to defeat armoured vehicles. The US army says the system can also be used against fortifications and other targets, giving infantry units a weapon that can be carried and operated close to the battlefield.One of the main advantages of Javelin is its fire-and-forget capability. The missile uses an imaging infrared seeker to guide itself after launch, allowing the operator to take cover or change position instead of continuously guiding the missile towards the target.The Javelin is produced by the Javelin Joint Venture between Raytheon and Lockheed Martin.The system consists of a reusable Command Launch Unit (CLU) and the missile, which is carried in a disposable launch tube. The CLU provides the operator with day and night sighting capabilities and can also be used independently for battlefield surveillance.The acquisition will give the army access to a proven anti-tank system while India continues to develop its own indigenous man-portable anti-tank missile. Javelin will help strengthen the army’s anti-armour capability in the meantime, providing an operational system that can be deployed without waiting for the indigenous missile programme to mature.

articles.title: A man spent his life’s earnings buying a 130-acre abandoned gravel pit, he planted 50,000 trees, and years later, the barren land had become a thriving wildlife oasis
articles.summary: UK News: Anthony Edmondson spent his life’s earnings buying a 130-acre abandoned gravel pit in the Cotswolds, south central England, in the 1980s. He planted 5.
articles.body: Anthony Edmondson spent his life’s earnings buying a 130-acre abandoned gravel pit in the Cotswolds, south central England, in the 1980s. He planted 50,000 trees, sowed wildflowers and added reeds to the water which over the years, has transformed the former industrial site into a landscape supporting birds and other wildlife.Edmondson’s decision was influenced by his time in Canada. Isabel Choat writes in The Guardian that Edmondson had worked in the silver mines of the Yukon and spent his time off staying in remote areas. When he returned to England and bought the former gravel pit, he wanted to recreate that feeling of wilderness closer to home.His work eventually helped the estate gain designation as a Site of Special Scientific Interest. Today, the property, known as Log House Holidays, has eight holiday cabins, each with access to the lake. The site combines accommodation and outdoor activities with the wildlife habitat Edmondson created.How barren land changedThe property lies near Pool Keynes, on the western edge of the Cotswolds Water Park. Edmondson’s 50,000 trees, wildflowers and reeds changed the character of the former gravel pit and created habitats for a wide range of wildlife.The Cotswolds is known for its rolling hills, fields, hedgerows and honey-coloured villages, but south of the Cotswolds Area of Outstanding Natural Beauty (AONB), the landscape also contains about 170 lakes.Most of these lakes were created about 50 years ago when gravel was extracted from the land. After the pits were no longer needed, many were bought by private owners or converted into nature reserves. The Cotswolds Water Park Trust now works to balance wildlife conservation with recreation across the area.Edmondson’s property is one of the quieter parts of this landscape. The lakes support wintering and breeding birds, while other parts of the wider Water Park are used for activities such as waterskiing and wakeboarding.Land becomes retreatThe natural landscape Edmondson created also became the setting for Log House Holidays. Visitors reach the cabins through an avenue of spruce before arriving at the lakes and woodland.The cabins were inspired by outback cabins in Canada but were imported from Finland. Built with chunky logs, they have underfloor heating supplied by a water pump. Each cabin also has its own rowing boat, giving visitors direct access to the lake.The lake and surrounding woodland have become an important part of the visitor experience. During an autumn visit, the changing colours of the trees were reflected in the water. A rowing trip offered opportunities to spot wildlife, although otters reportedly seen near the cabin did not appear.A heron was instead seen flying low over the water. The lake also provided a setting for the writer’s 10-year-old son to use the rowing boat independently.Visitors can also try activities including paddleboarding and kayaking. The wider Cotswolds Water Park has a mix of quieter wildlife sites and lakes used for watersports, making the former gravel pits part of both the area's natural environment and tourism industry.Choat describes how being surrounded by the landscape made the effect of nature particularly noticeable during the stay.Her family also visited nearby Cirencester when rain interrupted their outdoor plans. Its Corinium Museum contains Roman artefacts found in and around the area, including mosaics. They also visited the remains of what had once been one of Britain’s largest amphitheatres.The property is also close to Trewsbury Mead, a meadow identified as the source of the River Thames. The source is seasonal, meaning there may be no visible stream during dry weather. A large stone now marks the location. Before it was placed there in 1974, a statue of Father Thames marked the spot. A wooden signpost points towards the Thames Barrier, 184 miles away.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: In 2022, Melbourne's M80 became Victoria's first major road project with recycled content in every pavement layer, reusing 35.5 million plastic bags and 22 million bottles
articles.summary: Rest of World News: What if some of the waste we throw away could eventually become part of the roads we drive on? In 2022, Melbourne’s M80 Ring Road upgrade offered a st.
articles.body: What if some of the waste we throw away could eventually become part of the roads we drive on? In 2022, Melbourne’s M80 Ring Road upgrade offered a striking example of how discarded materials can be given another purpose through major infrastructure projects. The upgrade between Sydney Road and Edgars Road became Victoria’s first major road project to use recycled content in every layer of its pavement. According to Major Road Projects Victoria and Victoria’s Big Build, the project incorporated recycled material equivalent to 35.5 million plastic bags and more than 22 million glass bottles, as well as material equivalent to hundreds of thousands of toner cartridges and passenger car tyres. It also used thousands of tonnes of recycled pavement materials, including reclaimed asphalt, while more than 400,000 tonnes of material were recycled or sent for reuse. Beyond improving a busy section of Melbourne’s road network, the project demonstrated how waste materials could be redirected from landfill and incorporated into large-scale transport infrastructure.Recycled content throughoutThe key difference with the M80 upgrade was the extent to which recycled materials were used. Rather than incorporating recycled content into only one section of the road, the project used it throughout every pavement layer. According to Victoria’s Big Build, the Victorian Government’s program of major transport infrastructure projects, recycled materials made up more than 66% of the road’s composition. The materials included the equivalent of 35.5 million plastic bags and more than 22 million glass bottles.The project also reused material equivalent to around 800,000 toner cartridges and 820 passenger car tyres. These figures represent the equivalent amount of waste material incorporated into the construction rather than millions of individual waste items being directly placed into the pavement. This approach allowed materials that could otherwise have been discarded to become part of the infrastructure supporting one of Melbourne’s major transport routes.From waste to pavementThe recycled materials were not limited to plastics and glass. The project also extensively used recycled pavement materials. The May 2022 M80 Upgrade Construction Update, published by Major Road Projects Victoria, reported that approximately 51,000 tonnes of recycled pavement materials, including 14,000 tonnes of reclaimed asphalt, were used during the work. Another product used on the project was eMesh, an Australian-made reinforcement material containing 100% recycled plastic. More than 3.5 tonnes of eMesh were used as an alternative to traditional steel mesh and non-recycled plastic fibres. The construction update also reported that more than 400,000 tonnes of material from the project were recycled or sent to reuse facilities instead of being disposed of in landfill.A $518 million upgradeThe recycled-material initiative was part of a much larger project to improve the M80 Ring Road between Sydney Road and Edgars Road. The $518 million upgrade covered about four kilometres of the freeway and was designed to increase capacity, improve safety and make traffic movements more reliable. The works included new lanes, upgraded interchanges and ramps, as well as a smart freeway management system. The project also introduced ramp metering technology to help regulate vehicles entering the freeway and manage traffic flow. According to Major Road Projects Victoria, the upgraded section was expected to benefit more than 165,000 drivers each day. The new lanes and ramps opened progressively between November 2021 and March 2022, with the major works completed in 2022.Giving waste a new purposeThe M80 project demonstrated that recycled materials do not have to remain limited to small-scale construction or individual products. They can also be incorporated into large transport infrastructure. Using recycled materials can provide an alternative destination for waste that might otherwise go to landfill while reducing the need for newly sourced construction materials.For the M80 upgrade, the approach was particularly notable because recycled content was incorporated into every pavement layer. This made the project different from road projects where recycled materials may be used only in selected components. The figures also give a sense of the scale of the initiative. The equivalent of 35.5 million plastic bags and more than 22 million glass bottles were redirected into the project, alongside material from hundreds of thousands of toner cartridges and hundreds of passenger car tyres.A milestone for VictoriaThe M80 Ring Road upgrade was ultimately about improving Melbourne’s road network, but its construction also marked a significant milestone in how recycled materials could be used in major infrastructure. Major Road Projects Victoria described the M80 upgrade between Sydney Road and Edgars Road as Victoria’s first major road project to include recycled content in every layer of its pavement. The project offered a practical example of how materials commonly viewed as waste could be processed and incorporated into infrastructure. For millions of plastic bags and glass bottles, their journey did not necessarily end in a bin or landfill. Through the M80 upgrade, material equivalent to those discarded items became part of a major freeway project in Melbourne, showing how waste could be given another purpose on the road itself.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: In 1864, an Indian Maharaja built a 368-foot well in a drought-hit English village; the story behind Stoke Row’s ‘Maharaja’s Well’
articles.summary: Rest of World News: There is a small English village where an ornate well carries an Indian connection. In Stoke Row, Oxfordshire, stands the Maharaja’s Well, a 368-foot-.
articles.body: There is a small English village where an ornate well carries an Indian connection. In Stoke Row, Oxfordshire, stands the Maharaja’s Well, a 368-foot-deep water well funded by the Maharaja of Benares in the 1860s. It was built when the village was struggling with water shortages and was officially opened in 1864. The well was not built as a monument. It was meant to provide the villagers with a reliable source of water. The story behind it began thousands of kilometres away in India.How an English village came to the Maharaja's attentionStoke Row, in the Chiltern Hills, had limited access to reliable water. According to the British Geological Survey,the village’s location and local geology meant that water could become scarce during dry periods. Ponds could dry up, while the water table was deep underground.Historical accounts say that Edward Anderton Reade, a British official who had served in India, told the Maharaja of Benares about the difficulties faced by people in the village. One account says Reade told him about a child who had been punished after drinking the last available water at home during a period of drought. The story is presented in historical accounts as the incident that moved the Maharaja to help.According to BBC and some media reports, the Maharaja decided to fund a well in Stoke Row after hearing about the villagers' difficulties. The Maharaja was Ishwari Prasad Narayan Singh of Benares, who lived from 1822 to 1889. Historical references identify the project as a charitable gesture connected to his relationship with Reade.A well dug 368 feet into the groundWork on the well began in 1863. It was not a simple village well. The shaft was dug by hand to a depth of 368 feet (around 112 metres) to reach the water table. The British Geological Survey describes the depth as roughly the length of a standard football pitch. The local geology made the project particularly difficult because the secure water supply lay deep beneath the ground.The well cost £353 at the time (approximately ₹71,78,000 now), according to the British Geological Survey. Construction took about a year. The well was officially opened in 1864. But it did not look like an ordinary village water source.A golden elephant and an Indian-style pavilionThe well was eventually covered by an elaborate pavilion with an Anglo-Indian design. A golden elephant was placed above the well's winding machinery, giving the structure an unmistakable Indian connection. The British Geological Survey says the ornate wrought-iron pavilion and golden elephant remain a defining feature of the site. The structure was linked to the Maharaja in other ways too.A nearby cherry orchard, known as the Ishree Bagh, was established to help generate income for maintaining the well. The site also included a cottage for the person responsible for looking after it. The Maharaja never visited Stoke Row, but accounts say he continued to support the well and the village.The well changed the villageThe impact went beyond providing drinking water. Historical accounts say reliable access to water encouraged more people to settle in the village. Houses were built around the area and economic activity increased. The British Geological Survey notes that the Maharaja also planted the nearby cherry orchard as a source of income for the well's maintenance.The well remained an important source of water for decades. It eventually stopped being used for its original purpose after a proper water supply was brought to the village. A water pipeline arrived in 1927, after which the well gradually fell out of everyday use.The Maharaja's connection with the village continuedThe connection between Benares and Stoke Row did not end when the well was completed. According to few media reports, the Maharaja also helped the villagers during later difficulties. One such occasion came in 1882, after Queen Victoria survived an assassination attempt, when he funded provisions for the people of Stoke Row. The well itself became a lasting symbol of the relationship.In 1961, when the Maharaja of Benares met Queen Elizabeth II during her visit to India, the forthcoming centenary of the well was discussed, according to historical accounts. Three years later, Stoke Row held a centenary celebration.Prince Philip attended the centenaryOn April 8, 1964, nearly 1,500 people gathered in Stoke Row to mark 100 years of the well. Prince Philip, the Duke of Edinburgh, attended the celebration. A photograph from the event shows Prince Philip at the well as villagers gathered for the centenary celebrations. The occasion brought the story of the Indian-funded well back into public attention in Britain, 100 years after it had first been opened.Today, the Maharaja's Well remains in Stoke Row. The well no longer serves as the village's everyday water supply, but its pavilion, golden elephant and Indian associations remain. More than 160 years later, the Maharaja’s Well still stands as a reminder of an unusual connection between an Indian ruler and a distant English village.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: 3,000 years ago, 12 Bronze Age houses stood where a Scottish suburb is rising; archaeologists found graves, pottery kilns and food stores
articles.summary: UK News: More than 3,000 years ago, a community lived, worked and raised families on land that is now being transformed into a modern Scottish suburb. Archaeol.
articles.body: More than 3,000 years ago, a community lived, worked and raised families on land that is now being transformed into a modern Scottish suburb. Archaeologists excavating at Northbar, on the south-eastern outskirts of Erskine in Renfrewshire, discovered the remains of 12 Bronze Age roundhouses dating between 1500 and 1100 BC. The settlement contained evidence of farming, animal keeping, pottery production and weaving, and nearby graves revealed that the site had been used for burial centuries before the houses appeared. The excavation also uncovered charred crops, animal bones and large quantities of hazelnut shells, hinting at concerns over food shortages. Although the settlement eventually disappeared without obvious destruction, its remains provide a detailed glimpse into everyday life, work and hardship in Bronze Age Scotland.Discovery beneath the modern housing development in ScotlandThe archaeological remains were discovered by GUARD Archaeology(an independent commercial archaeological organisation based in Glasgow, Scotland) during excavations carried out during 2018-19. The work was commissioned by CALA Homes (a major British housebuilding company that designs and builds new residential properties across the UK) before construction began at Northbar, with the investigation required as part of the planning process. According to GUARD Archaeology, the site was occupied between 1500 and 1100 BC. Archaeologists identified 12 roundhouses spread across the area, showing that people returned to and developed the settlement over several centuries.The houses themselves had largely disappeared. Time, weather and later activity had destroyed the timber structures, leaving behind features such as post-holes and trenches. But those surviving marks were enough to reveal the scale of some buildings. GUARD Archaeology reported that several had been extremely large timber structures, capable of housing large groups of people. The discovery is significant because it does more than show where people lived. The remains also preserve clues about how those communities survived.Occupation of the Bronze Age people living at NorthbarThe people who lived at Northbar were closely connected to the surrounding landscape. Burnt animal bones and charred grains of barley and wheat found inside the roundhouses indicate that farming was an important part of life. Animal dung discovered in two of the houses provides another personal detail. According to GUARD Archaeology, people and animals may have shared the same buildings at certain times of the year. That arrangement would have been practical for a farming community. Keeping animals close could have provided warmth and made it easier to protect valuable livestock, although it would also have made daily life considerably less comfortable by modern standards.The discovery of large quantities of hazelnut shells adds another dimension to the story. GUARD Archaeology suggests that the nuts may have been collected and stored during autumn as a reserve food supply for the winter. Such preparation could have become particularly important if the grain harvest failed. The archaeologists point to evidence of famine and catastrophe at other Bronze Age communities in south-west Scotland, suggesting that the threat of food shortages was a genuine concern for people living at the time.Evidence of pottery and clothing at this Scottish siteThe settlement was not simply a farming community. Archaeologists found evidence that people produced some of the everyday objects they needed themselves. Several kiln pits were discovered inside one of the roundhouses. GUARD Archaeology describes these as rare evidence for pottery manufacture during this period. The kilns indicate that people at Northbar were making ceramic vessels, which could then be used for cooking and storing food. The discovery of numerous ‘clay loom weights’ provides evidence of weaving. Loom weights were used to keep the threads of a vertical loom under tension. Their presence at Northbar suggests that wool was being turned into cloth, probably for clothing and other household purposes. Together, they show a community capable of producing basic necessities rather than relying entirely on goods brought in from elsewhere. GUARD Archaeology notes that Bronze Age communities were connected to one another, but the evidence from Northbar demonstrates a considerable degree of self-sufficiency.Mystery behind the burials at Northbar The story of Northbar goes back even further than the roundhouses. Several centuries before the settlement was established, part of the site had already been used as a cemetery during the Early Bronze Age. GUARD Archaeology discovered cremated human remains belonging to at least nine people. Fragments of ‘ceramic Beakers and urns’ were also found alongside the cremated remains. These objects had been placed with the dead, apparently as part of burial practices intended to accompany them into the afterlife. The presence of the cemetery raises an intriguing possibility. GUARD Archaeology reports that the earlier graves and reputation of the people buried there may have influenced why a later community chose to settle in the same location. That possibility cannot be proven, but it gives the landscape a deeper history. For the people who built the roundhouses, the ground may have carried meaning because of those who had been buried there generations earlier.Why did the Bronze Age settlement disappearBy around 1100 BC, the settlement at Northbar came to an end. There was no clear evidence that the houses had been destroyed by fire or deliberately attacked. GUARD Archaeology notes that other Bronze Age settlements in Scotland, including sites at Rosemarkie on the Black Isle and Carnoustie in Angus, also came to an end around the close of the Bronze Age. This suggests that the abandonment of Northbar may have been part of a wider change in how communities occupied the landscape. After the Bronze Age settlement disappeared, there was little evidence of human activity at the site for a very long time.What does the discovery reveal about Bronze Age ScotlandThe Northbar excavation offers a remarkably human picture of a community that existed thousands of years before the modern houses being built there. The remains reveal people farming wheat and barley, keeping animals, gathering wild food, making pottery and weaving wool. The graves show that the landscape had also been used by earlier generations for burial. The evidence of hazelnut storage hints at people preparing for difficult times perhaps. Food shortages could threaten a household, so gathering and storing wild resources may have been one way to prepare for an uncertain winter. As reported by GUARD Archaeology, the archaeological work is now complete. The artefacts will enter the Scottish Treasure Trove system and be allocated to an appropriate museum. Underneath a modern suburb, the excavation has preserved the traces of a community that lived, worked, worried about food and buried its dead more than three millennia ago.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Oracle layoffs: Company leadership may again send the '6 am' email on September 1 that told employees, "We have made the decision to…
articles.summary: Tech News News: Oracle employees have spent the last three weeks watching a calendar instead of a dashboard. The company has drawn up plans for another round of job c.
articles.body: Oracle employees have spent the last three weeks watching a calendar instead of a dashboard. The company has drawn up plans for another round of job cuts, managers have been asked to submit lists of employees whose roles could be eliminated, and the target is to bring payroll down by September 1, the day Oracle's fiscal second quarter opens. Business Insider first reported the plan, citing people familiar with it and an internal document, and said reductions on some teams could run into double-digit percentages. Oracle declined to comment and has not confirmed anything publicly.Employees now expect the emails to land on the morning of September 1 itself, an expectation that comes from the workforce rather than the company, built on how the last round went. On March 31, thousands of Oracle staff in the US, India, Canada and Mexico woke up at roughly 6 am local time to a note from "Oracle Leadership" that opened with a line about sharing difficult news regarding their position. It said that after careful consideration of Oracle's current business needs, the company had decided to eliminate the role as part of a broader organisational change, and that as a result, today was their last working day. It thanked them for their dedication and impact. Then it told them severance would follow only after they signed termination paperwork, arriving via DocuSign at the Oracle email address they were about to lose access to. There was no HR call and no manager conversation. System access was revoked the same morning.Oracle employees are refreshing inboxes at 6 am, and swapping dates on RedditThe waiting has produced its own strange rituals. On r/employeesOfOracle, a 52,000-visitor forum that has run a "probable layoff" megathread through August, one employee described checking email at 6 am on the Monday after payday just to confirm he still had a job. Another noted that nothing had landed at 6 am at Oracle's India Development Centre, and reasoned that if the US wave hit first, IDC would follow the next morning, which is roughly how March played out.The rumours have moved around. Some in the thread now expect September 15, pointing to a townhall scheduled that day. Others say after September 24 or 25. Employees in Fusion IDC flagged something odder: several managers at M4 and M6 level took leave from August 24 through September 1, with one poster claiming August 24 was the internal deadline for budget allocation. None of it is confirmed, and the sub's own rules ban unverified layoff rumours, which tells you how much of this is circulating.One longer post tried to impose order on the panic by listing patterns from earlier rounds: the quarterly townhall tends to come before the cuts, rumours start two to three weeks ahead, and there is never a single global date because labour laws differ by region.Why Oracle's RSU vesting calendar is part of the layoff conversationThe other pattern employees keep returning to is stock. Restricted stock units make up a large slice of engineering pay at Oracle, and unvested RSUs are forfeited on exit. A survey of 272 workers cut in March found 27% had stock due to vest within 90 days. One laid-off senior manager said 70% of his compensation sat in RSUs and he was four months from $1 million vesting.That history is why the Reddit thread is full of people counting down to their own vest dates in September, October and November, and asking whether acceleration is negotiable. The consensus answer from those already cut is no. One ex-employee said a group took Oracle to court seeking 2026 RSUs be honoured and lost.Oracle has already cut 21,000 jobs in one fiscal yearThis would be a continuation, not a fresh start. Oracle's headcount fell by about 21,000 in the fiscal year ended May 31, roughly 13% of its workforce, taking the company from around 162,000 to about 141,000, of whom roughly 49,000 are in the US. Restructuring costs jumped to $1.8 billion from $374 million a year earlier, a 391% increase.There is not much budget left. Oracle's 10-K, filed June 22, capped the total expected cost of its FY2026 restructuring plan at $2.1 billion. With $1.8 billion booked, that leaves about $300 million of headroom. Cuts on the scale Business Insider describes would either squeeze into that remainder or push Oracle into its second new restructuring plan in three years.Why the $55.7 billion AI data centre bill keeps squeezing Oracle's payrollThe arithmetic is not subtle. Capital expenditure hit $55.7 billion in FY2026, up from $21.2 billion the year before, mostly on data centres for AI customers including OpenAI. Oracle burned $23.7 billion more cash than it generated, raised $43 billion in debt and $5 billion in equity, and expects about $40 billion more this year. Interest expense alone climbed to $4.6 billion from $3.6 billion.TD Cowen estimated in January that cutting 20,000 to 30,000 roles could free up $8-10 billion in incremental free cash flow. Seven months on, that reads less like a forecast and more like a plan.Oracle revenue is up 17%, which is exactly why these layoffs stingOn paper this is not a struggling company. FY2026 revenue rose 17% to $67.4 billion, cloud infrastructure revenue grew 77%, and remaining performance obligations closed the year at $638 billion. Oracle's own annual filing links part of the headcount decline to its adoption of AI, the same technology it is borrowing tens of billions to sell. The stock disagrees, down more than 20% this year, with shareholders suing in January over what Oracle said about the borrowing needed for its $300 billion OpenAI commitment.For employees on this month's lists, the only unknown left is the hour the email arrives.Get the latest technology news and updates. articles.title: 2 shooters, 2-day hotel stay and a GPS device: New leads emerge in Ankit Baliyan murder
articles.summary: SHAMLI: CCTV footage showing two men involved in the murder of Haryanvi singer Ankit Baliyan checking into a hotel barely 1.5km from the crime scene o.
articles.body: SHAMLI: CCTV footage showing two men involved in the murder of Haryanvi singer Ankit Baliyan checking into a hotel barely 1.5km from the crime scene on August 20 has emerged as a key lead in the investigation, officials said.The footage shows the two suspected shooters arriving on a motorbike and enter Hotel Surya in the area. The video purportedly shows one of them making payment in cash at the hotel reception while the other looks on.Police suspect the stay formed part of a larger plan to track Ankit Baliyan and execute the attack.According to the investigation, the two suspects stayed at the hotel for two days and submitted their identity cards and PAN details at the time of check-in.Police said that the duo had also allegedly brought a GPS device with them, which investigators suspect was intended to be fitted in a vehicle to track movements.However, the police said, the device could not be installed.Investigators believe the accused were able to monitor Ankit Baliyan’s movements through his regular visits to the gym and his social media updates.According to police, members and supporters of the Gogi gang allegedly believed that Ankit Baliyan’s appearance in a song had brought disrepute to the gang.The investigation has also revealed that the gang had allegedly been trying to locate a target earlier and had threatened him, but he remained cautious, reduced his movement and stayed out of sight for several months.According to investigators, the two accused seen at the hotel later joined two other shooters on August 26.Police said Bholu Sapuria allegedly supplied the weapons to the group on the day of the murder. Two youths reportedly arrived from the Karnal side and two from Sonipat before the group carried out the attack.Ankit Baliyan was shot dead outside a gym in Shamli on August 26. Police had earlier said four assailants opened fire on him before fleeing the spot.Nine bullets, including .30 and .32 calibre rounds, were recovered from the crime scene, according to the investigation. Police believe the recovered weapons may have been used in the murder, although a forensic examination is required to establish a match.The latest leads follow Monday’s encounter in which two accused, Sumit and Mohit, were killed by police in Shamli.The duo, both allegedly linked to the Gogi gang and residents of Sonipat, had rewards of Rs 50,000 each on their heads, police said.According to officials, the two had fled towards Loni via Baghpat after the murder and were intercepted while attempting to travel towards Sonipat through Shamli’s industrial area.Police said the accused opened fire on the police team, prompting retaliatory firing. Both were injured and later declared dead at a hospital. Two policemen were also injured in the exchange.With Sumit and Mohit killed, police teams are continuing the search for the remaining accused, Satyam and Aryan.Investigators are examining CCTV footage, hotel records, social media activity and other evidence to establish the sequence of events and identify everyone involved in the murder.You Can Also Check: Gold Rate in Lucknow | Silver Rate in Lucknow | Bank Holidays in Lucknow | Public Holidays in Lucknow | Lucknow AQI | Weather in Lucknow | Petrol Price in Lucknow | Diesel Price in Lucknow | CNG Price in Lucknow | LPG Price in LucknowStay updated with the latest Lucknow news. articles.title: PM Modi's jackets, Rahul's shirts, Mamata's sarees: How leaders use fashion for political messaging
articles.summary: India News: From Indira Gandhi's sarees to Narendra Modi's carefully curated bandhgalas, from Rajiv Gandhi's sneakers and sunglasses to the Thackerays' colour-cod.
articles.body: From Indira Gandhi's sarees to Narendra Modi's carefully curated bandhgalas, from Rajiv Gandhi's sneakers and sunglasses to the Thackerays' colour-coded political imagery, what Indian politicians wear has often been more than a question of personal style. Their clothes have helped construct identities, signal ideology, project modernity, invoke tradition and increasingly generate the kind of visual moments that social media loves.So when Rahul Gandhi appeared in a pink shirt and later in a yellow one, the change from his usual white clothing drew attention online. The yellow shirt, along with the line "Smash the patriarchy", became part of the social-media conversation. The interest was less about the shirt itself and more about how unusual it looked compared with his regular public appearance.But this is not the first time that a politician's attire has made more headlines than their speech. Prime Minister Narendra Modi's clothes have often drawn attention, from his signature jackets and bandhgalas to the regional outfits he wears during visits across the country. Over the years, they have become a familiar part of his public image.As designer Gaurav Jai Gupta puts it, "Fashion can communicate before a politician has spoken a single word. Clothing conveys identity, ideology, relatability, authority and even regional or cultural affiliation almost instantly." Politics, he adds, is fundamentally about perception, and "an outfit can become the visual shorthand for an entire political moment.PM Modi: How his wardrobe became part of his public imagePrime Minister Narendra Modi has taken political dressing into the era of personal branding.His wardrobe moves easily between traditional Indian clothing and sharply tailored modern silhouettes. The signature kurta, sleeveless jackets and bandhgalas have become instantly recognisable, while his international appearances often combine Indian craftsmanship with global tailoring.Some of the looks have become headline-makers in their own right.In January 2015, during his meetings with then-US President Barack Obama, Modi wore a pinstriped bandhgala whose stripes, on closer inspection, repeatedly carried his full name — "Narendra Damodardas Modi" — embroidered into the fabric.His wardrobe has since offered plenty of other visual moments.A burgundy bandhgala during his first overseas trip as prime minister created a polished diplomatic look. A signature khadi kurta during his Bhutan visit emphasised Indian textiles and craftsmanship. In Nepal, saffron attire paired with a rudraksh mala made a strong cultural and religious statement at Pashupatinath Temple.This habit of dressing for the country he's visiting — or the region of India he's in — is itself a strategy, according to Gupta: "I would definitely consider it a form of fashion diplomacy. Clothing can be a very subtle way of acknowledging the culture of the country you are visiting while siultaneously representing your own identity." Retaining elements of one's own traditional identity alongside that, he says, "reinforces national representation."His recent looks have been more state-centric. From sporting the gamcha look in Bihar, to a turban in Punjab, and even the traditional mund in Kerala, Modi has worn his "vocals for locals" tag.Pink, yellow, blue – Rahul's pattern?For years, Rahul Gandhi's public wardrobe has largely stayed within the safe territory of political dressing — white kurta-pajamas, jackets and understated casual wear. It is a familiar uniform in Indian politics, one that keeps the focus on the politician rather than the clothes.But the pink and yellow shirts were different.Bright, instantly noticeable and far removed from the monochrome political wardrobe, they became an unlikely talking point. Gupta explains why a single garment can take on a life entirely of its own online: "The internet loves symbols that are simple, recognisable and easy to reproduce. A yellow shirt is, in itself, just a yellow shirt. But once social media attaches a narrative to it, the garment can acquire an entirely new meaning." The audience, he says, effectively co-authors the outfit's significance — "memes, edits, captions and commentary can transform an ordinary look into a cultural reference point," helped along by the fact that "colour is highly emotional and visually immediate."He did not wear it just anywhere, either. He wore it to the 'Chhatron ki Goonj' programme, where the audience was predominantly Gen Z. But this is not the first time the Leader of Opposition has made news for his fashion. In 2019, Rahul attended a Kerala college event in a t-shirt and jeans, taking a break from his classic white kurta look, with his "You can call me Rahul" reels still going viral.Likewise, it was not a conincidence that he went with a blue t-shirt, when he held up the red book in his hand and said "Save the Constitution", or a black one to protest outside the Parliament.It's a pattern. Every Rahul Gandhi's politics has reflected in his preference for colours.Indira Gandhi: The saree that became a power statementLong before politicians had to worry about going viral, Indira Gandhi had already mastered the art of having a recognisable political look.Her sarees, from Banarasi silk to handlooms and Tanchois, became an important part of her public image. They projected tradition and authority at the same time, allowing her to appear deeply rooted in Indian culture while commanding political spaces at home and abroad.The saree wasn't simply a sartorial choice. The way she wore it, with the pallu covering her head from the loose end of the saree, made it distinct.Gupta points to exactly this kind of repetition as the foundation of a political fashion identity: "Consistency is the key to creating a fashion identity. When a politician repeatedly wears a particular silhouette, colour palette, accessory or garment, it becomes part of their visual vocabulary." Indira Gandhi's sarees, he notes, "became inseparable from her public image," much "like branding in fashion or advertising: repetition creates recognition." Eventually, he says, "you don't need to see the entire person; a particular silhouette, colour combination or accessory can be enough to trigger recognition." But he's careful to add a caveat: "successful political style usually feels authentic rather than overly constructed. The strongest personal brands emerge when the clothes reinforce something the politician already represents."For women in politics especially, clothing has always carried an extra layer of scrutiny. Too traditional, and a leader can be boxed into convention. Too Western, and questions about cultural authenticity can follow.Moreover, most female political leaders of the time or the ones who preceeded her wore sarees the same way.Indira's style largely sidestepped that binary. She made traditional Indian clothing look powerful.Nehru's jacket, Rajiv's sneakers: Political wardrobe evolvesThe political fashion story goes back even further.Jawaharlal Nehru's iconic jacket became so closely associated with him that his name effectively became part of the garment's identity. The jacket was a descendant of the northern Indian achkan, a closed-neck, coat-like garment traditionally associated with Indian nobility. It was largely when the style was marketed to Western audiences that it took the "Nehru" name, after the prime minister popularised it through his public appearances. The minimalist look later found fans beyond politics, including the Beatles and Sammy Davis Jr, who reportedly owned more than 200 Nehru jackets.Khadi and handlooms carried an even bigger political history, associated with nationalism, self-reliance and the freedom movement.Then came Rajiv Gandhi.Dark sunglasses, sneakers, sleeveless fleece jackets and khadi kurta-pajamas gave him a distinctly more contemporary appearance. His wardrobe reflected the image he projected politically — younger, modern and more comfortable with the technological future.In other parts of the world, political leaders also turned their clothes into signatures. Mao Zedong's four-pocketed tunic, known as the Zhongshan suit and later the Mao suit, became closely associated with communist China and was brought back into fashion during his rule. Usually seen in muted shades of grey, green or blue, the suit became a visual shorthand for Mao and communism before falling out of favour after his death in 1976.The Thackerays: When colour carries politicsIf PM Modi's wardrobe demonstrates the power of personal branding, the Thackerays show how colour and clothing can become political shorthand.Bal Thackeray initially adopted the shirt-and-trouser look of the urban office worker, appealing to an aspirational Maharashtra audience. Later, as Hindutva became central to his political positioning, orange became a defining element of his public appearance.Fashion designer Nivedita Saboo, who has dressed several politicians, explains why colour carries this kind of political weight in the first place: "Colour communicates emotion before language does. Saffron can evoke spirituality, sacrifice, nationalism and Hindu cultural identity. White can communicate simplicity, peace, authority or the traditional Gandhian vocabulary. Electric or deep blue has powerful associations with social justice, equality and Ambedkarite politics." But, she cautions, "colour is never universal. Its meaning changes with culture, history, political association, fabric, styling and even the person's body language. That's why political dressing is fascinating: you can say something without saying anything."Uddhav Thackeray developed his own visual identity through simple, brightly coloured sadra-pajamas closely associated with Maharashtrian culture.Aaditya Thackeray, meanwhile, represents another generational shift, combining traditional Indian clothing with contemporary fashion.Three generations. Three styles. And three different ways of speaking to their audiences without saying a word.Mamata, Kejriwal and the politics of looking 'aam'Then there are politicians whose biggest fashion statement is that they appear to have made very little effort at all.Mamata Banerjee's white cotton saree with a blue border and hawai chappals have become almost inseparable from her political identity. Arvind Kejriwal's muffler achieved a similar status.The appeal is simple: don't look like a politician; look like the people who vote for you. As Gupta puts it, "politics is about recognition and relatability, not necessarily luxury." A consistent, uncomplicated look, he says, "can become incredibly powerful because people can immediately identify it" — Mamata Banerjee's saree and Kejriwal's muffler "function almost like logos," communicating accessibility in a way an expensive designer wardrobe rarely can. "In a country like ours, simplicity is more relatable," he says. "In mass politics, that emotional connection can be far more valuable than sartorial sophistication."The repetition is what makes it powerful. Eventually, the garment becomes a logo.See the white-and-blue saree, think Mamata. See the muffler, think Kejriwal. See the kurta and jacket, think Modi.And now, in the age of viral fashion moments, perhaps even a yellow shirt can enter the political visual dictionary.Vijay: Breaking Tamil Nadu's white-shirt, veshti political dress codeWhen Vijay took oath as Tamil Nadu chief minister, he broke from the traditional white shirt-and-veshti look, arriving instead in a sharply tailored black suit. He has since made black-and-white suits a regular part of his public image.Addressing the attention around his wardrobe, Vijay said, “Many people have been talking about the new suit that I have been wearing recently. Are we not allowed to wear a coat and suit? Is it meant only for people in positions of authority? There is nothing like that.”Explaining his choice, he added, “I am not wearing many colours. It is just black and white, like all our hearts. The choice of these colours is to show that I will remain transparent and simple in everything, just like black and white.”Mao & Castro: The outfit of revolutionariesIn other parts of the world, political leaders also turned their clothes into signatures. Mao Zedong's four-pocketed tunic, known as the Zhongshan suit and later the Mao suit, became closely associated with communist China and was brought back into fashion during his rule. Usually seen in muted shades of grey, green or blue, the suit became a visual shorthand for Mao and communism before falling out of favour after his death in 1976.Fidel Castro, meanwhile, swapped the traditional military and political imagery for tracksuits later in life. He was famously photographed wearing a red, white and blue Adidas tracksuit while recovering from surgery in 2006. The look soon became part of his public image, with Castro later wearing sportswear from brands including Fila, Puma and Nike.What would it take to dress for Gen Z?If a yellow shirt at a college event can trend for days, the question naturally follows: what does it actually take for a politician's wardrobe to land with a generation raised on Instagram and short-form video?Saboo, who has worked closely with politicians on exactly this brief, is blunt about the trap most of them fall into. "Gen Z has grown up in a visual culture where identity is communicated through what you wear," she says. "But breaking the dress code simply to look young can backfire. Gen Z is extremely good at detecting what feels manufactured. The clothes have to feel like the person, not like a stylist has dressed them to look young." A politician who "wears the traditional kurta beautifully and owns it completely," she argues, can be "far more compelling than somebody wearing sneakers and a T-shirt because someone told them that's what young people like." For her, the real shift isn't from tradition to trend — it's "from dress code to personal code."Asked to imagine one outfit that could say "young India" without a single slogan, she describes something quietly hybrid: a relaxed, engineered jacket in a lightweight Indian textile over a tapered trouser, perhaps a modernised kurta with sharper, almost architectural proportions underneath, finished with one unexpected element — an unusual seam, a technical fabric panel, a monogram, a contemporary sneaker. The palette, she says, would be "sophisticated rather than loud — ivory, charcoal, deep blue or earthy neutrals with one energetic accent." The test, in her words: "It shouldn't look like 'politician trying to be fake and dress young.' It should look like India's next generation has naturally evolved its own version of Indian clothing."Her advice to politicians boils down to five principles: don't dress younger, dress more authentically; modernise proportions rather than identity; find one recurring signature — a colour, a silhouette, a jacket, a watch — rather than constantly changing the wardrobe; make sure the clothes actually function in a country that "lives fast"; and, above all, stop being afraid of personality. As she puts it, "politics has traditionally rewarded conformity. Gen Z is attracted to people who appear comfortable in their own skin." Fashion, she concludes, "cannot manufacture relatability. It can only amplify it."Get the latest India News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Scientists reconstructed the face of ‘Conquest Man’, a 1,000-year-old skeleton buried just 13 years after the Norman Conquest
articles.summary: Rest of World News: More than 1,000 years after his death, a man who lived through the upheaval of the Norman Conquest has been given a face. Known as “Conquest Man”, he .
articles.body: More than 1,000 years after his death, a man who lived through the upheaval of the Norman Conquest has been given a face. Known as “Conquest Man”, he was buried at St Peter’s Church in Barton-upon-Humber, Lincolnshire, around 1079, just 13 years after William the Conqueror’s victory at Hastings. New research has combined osteological analysis, ancient DNA, isotope testing and digital facial reconstruction to investigate who he may have been and where he came from. The study, led by English Heritage with researchers from Historic England, the Francis Crick Institute, British Geological Survey, University of Southampton, muVIS and Face Lab at Liverpool John Moores University, points to a man with connections extending beyond England. His reconstructed face now offers a strikingly personal glimpse into a period usually told through kings, battles and political upheaval.Who was the man buried in a Norman-owned church?The Conquest Man was a stocky, muscular man who stood just over five feet tall and was between 50 and 60 years old when he died. His skeleton contains evidence of several healed fractures, indicating that he had experienced significant injuries during his lifetime but survived them. His burial also suggests that he held a degree of status within the community. His oak coffin has been dated to around 1079, placing his burial only a little over a decade after the Norman Conquest. He was laid to rest with his arms folded, his head resting on a grass pillow and two pieces of local chalk positioned to prevent it from falling sideways. Three applewood staffs were also placed beside him, adding an unusual Scandinavian element to the burial. The church itself adds another layer to his story. St Peter’s was a pre-Conquest church that became associated with the Norman elite and was owned by one of William the Conqueror’s knights. Conquest Man was therefore buried in a church connected to the new ruling order while retaining burial practices linked to an older Scandinavian tradition. According to English Heritage, the coordinator of the study, Kevin Booth, said the individual had fascinated him for around 20 years. Booth explained that the new analysis has allowed researchers to get much closer to understanding the man, while also challenging the simplistic idea that people living through the Conquest could be divided neatly into “Saxon” and “Norman” groups.Ancient DNA reveals a man with a much more complex heritageThe research went beyond examining Conquest Man’s bones. Scientists used ancient DNA and isotope analysis alongside osteological evidence to investigate his ancestry and movements. The results indicate that he had substantial ancestry from continental Europe, suggesting that his biological background was connected to a much wider geographical area than medieval England alone. The isotope evidence provides further clues about his childhood and later life. English Heritage reports that oxygen levels in one of his teeth are consistent with him having spent his adolescence in a colder climate, while his strontium isotope results are more compatible with the region around Barton-upon-Humber later in his life. The evidence does not, however, identify a precise birthplace. Dr Sarah Stark, Human Skeletal Biologist at Historic England via EH, said the scientific evidence does not point towards one straightforward homeland for the individual. Instead, his skeleton, burial, ancient DNA and isotope results indicate a man connected to the wider continental world. He may have travelled to Barton, she explained, or he may have been born locally within a community already shaped by those connections. The findings also complicate the way the Norman Conquest is often presented. England already had strong Scandinavian influences by the 11th century, while Normandy itself had significant Scandinavian connections. Conquest Man’s background therefore reflects a Europe in which populations, cultures and identities were already intertwined long before and after 1066.Face Lab digitally reconstructed the face of Conquest ManAfter the scientific investigation, Face Lab at Liverpool John Moores University used the evidence preserved in Conquest Man’s skull to create a digital facial reconstruction. For the first time, researchers and the public can move beyond his anonymous skeleton and see an approximation of the person who lived during the Norman Conquest. The facial depiction is credited to Face Lab, Liverpool John Moores University.The reconstruction shows an older man with receding, greying hair and facial stubble, bringing a remarkably human dimension to archaeological evidence that had previously consisted largely of bones and burial remains. It is important, however, to understand the image as a scientifically informed reconstruction rather than an exact portrait. The significance lies partly in what Conquest Man was not. He was not a king, famous warrior or member of the Norman aristocracy whose likeness was preserved in medieval art. He appears to have been an ordinary person who lived through one of the defining political transformations in English history. The collaboration between English Heritage, Historic England, the Francis Crick Institute, British Geological Survey, University of Southampton, muVIS and Face Lab demonstrates how several scientific disciplines can now be combined to reconstruct an individual's life centuries after written records have disappeared.What Conquest Man reveals about life after the Norman ConquestThe new findings make Conquest Man significant not simply because scientists can now reconstruct his face, but because his story challenges the idea of a straightforward divide between the people living in England before and after 1066. His DNA, burial objects and possible movements point towards a society with Anglo-Saxon, Scandinavian and continental European connections. His burial is particularly revealing. Scandinavian-associated objects were placed beside him, yet his final resting place was a privileged burial within a church belonging to the new Norman world. Rather than showing two completely separate cultures, the evidence suggests that different traditions could coexist within the same community.There is still no evidence that Conquest Man fought at the Battle of Hastings, travelled to England with William’s army or belonged to a particular political faction. Researchers have deliberately avoided assigning him a definitive identity because the available evidence cannot support such conclusions. What can be established is that he survived the upheaval and lived into the period when Norman rule was becoming established. As Booth of English Heritage puts it, Conquest Man represents “survival, resilience and adaptation”. His reconstructed face consequently does more than put an image to an ancient skeleton. It reminds us that the Norman Conquest was experienced by individuals whose lives were far more complicated than the simple “Saxon versus Norman” story often associated with 1066.Catch the latest World News and Live updates.
